title: Detroit Lions vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers preview, prediction: On Paper
summary: For the first time in several weeks, the Detroit Lions hold the top spot in the NFC North. But in order to hold it, they’ll have to take down a sneaky-good Tampa Bay Buccaneers team. They may be 3-6 on the season, but as you’ll soon see, they are doing a lot of things very […]
full_text: Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield (6) hugs Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) at the end of the Detroit Lions game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 15, 2024. Buccaneers won 20-16. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co For the first time in several weeks, the Detroit Lions hold the top spot in the NFC North. But in order to hold it, they’ll have to take down a sneaky-good Tampa Bay Buccaneers team. They may be 3-6 on the season, but as you’ll soon see, they are doing a lot of things very well, and present a tough matchup for any team. There’s a reason why they have a positive point differential, despite having two times the losses than wins. I’ll break it down further in my Detroit Lions vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers preview and prediction: On Paper. Lions pass offense (11th) vs. Bucs pass defense (3rd) The Lions’ passing attack remains pretty steady and reliable, despite the fact that Jared Goff has now thrown an interception in three straight games after not throwing a single one through his first six contests. For the year, the Lions rank: Sixth in yards per attempt (8.0) Fifth in passer rating (106.0) Fifth in dropback EPA (0.200) Fifth in success rate (49.9%) In short, the Lions have been playing like a near top-five passing offense pretty much all season. Goff is at his best when his offensive line is pass blocking for him, and the front has done a pretty good job this year. Detroit is allowing just a 30.8% pressure rate (fifth best) and 6.4% sack rate (15th), while ranking fourth in pass block win rate (58%) and second in PFF pass blocking grade (76.8). Relevant this week is how Goff performs against the blitz, seeing as Tampa blitzes at the second-highest rate in the NFL. This year against the blitz, the Goff ranks: Fifth in passer rating (115.6) Fourth in EPA/dropback (+0.19) Sixth in yards per pass attempt (8.2) So blitz at your own peril. The Bucs have shut down nearly every single opponent this year in the passing game, outside of—oddly—Deshaun Watson. For the year, they rank: 11th in yards per attempt (6.6) Second in passer rating (72.7) Second in dropback EPA (-0.101) Eighth in success rate (43.3%) Obviously, these stats are pretty darn good, but with lower success rates and yards per attempt than EPA and passer rating, there’s at least a little indication that some of these stats are being propped up by Tampa’s ridiculous 16 interceptions (most in NFL) and 5.2 interception rate (highest). While the Bucs deserve credit for those interceptions, a 5.2% interception rate is unbelievably high. The highest interception rate for an entire season over the past 10 years is 4.7%. There’s a good chance this is unsustainable. Regardless, this is still a top-10 pass defense and shouldn’t be overlooked. As mentioned earlier, the Bucs have the second-highest blitz rate (43.9%), yet their pressure rate ranks just 24th (33.2%) and their sack rate is 25th (5.0%) per NFL Pro. That said, they are improving as the season goes on. Of their 17 sacks on the season, 11 have come in the last four games. Really, their pass defense is led by a strong secondary. Cornerbacks Jacob Parish, Zyon McCullom, and rookie nickel Keionte Scott are having outstanding seasons. Player to watch: Rueben Bain Jr. vs. Blake Miller. Who isn’t excited about first-round rookie on rookie action? Bain and Miller were taken two spots apart, and both have had ups and downs in their rookie season. Bain is starting to put some things together after a slow start to his career, while Miller has seen more good than bad. Advantage: Lions +0.5. With all due respect to DVOA, I think the Bucs’ numbers are a little artificially inflated by high interception rates. I still think it’s going to be a slog for the Lions to put up big numbers, but I won’t be surprised if they can patiently dink and dunk their way down the field. Lions run offense (2nd) vs. Bucs run defense (5th) Every week, the Lions’ run game gets a little more consistent and explosive. For the year, Detroit ranks: Eighth in yards per carry (4.6) 10th in rush EPA (-0.021) Second in success rate (47.1%) What’s even more promising is that the high stuffed rate that had been plaguing this rushing attack is finally starting to settle down. Right now it sits at 18.6%, which is still 10th-highest, but it’s on a downward trajectory. Similarly, their power success rate is much better now. After Week 8, the Lions were converting on just 59% of short yardage situations (24th). Now they’re at 68% (12th). It’s been a marriage between good blocking and Jahmyr Gibbs being outstanding. The Lions rank second in adjusted line yards (4.99), seventh in run block win rate (75%), and fourth in PFF run-blocking grade (77.0). Meanwhile, Gibbs has forced 16 more missed tackles than any other player and is averaging 3.6 yards after contact per rush (11th). Put it all together and Detroit is both extremely consistent down to down (see: success rate) and explosive (second-most 10+ yard runs in the NFL). The Lions may have met their match this week. The Bucs haven’t allowed over 100 rushing yards since Week 1, and only two opponents all year have managed 4.0 yards per carry or more against this unit. For the year, they rank: Third in yards per carry allowed (3.5) Third in rush EPA (-0.145) Second in success rate (34.9%) It’s hard to pick holes in the data here. Tampa is legit. They don’t give up big plays (only 16 rushes of 10+ yards, third fewest). The defensive line ranks well in run-stop win rate (eight), adjusted line yards (seventh), and second in PFF run-defense grade. Player to watch: Josiah Trotter. The second-round rookie linebacker has been outstanding for the Bucs’ defense, ranking 19th in PFF run defense grade among qualifying linebackers. He leads the team in tackles (76) and PFF run stops (14). Advantage: Draw. It’s elite vs. elite, and both teams have shown they can win those kind of matchups. Detroit ran all over the elite Vikings’ run defense, while the Bucs completely shut down both the Falcons and Bears strong rushing attacks. I can’t pick a side here. Bucs pass offense (26th) vs. Lions pass defense (19th) Bold and italicized data were starts by Jalen Daniels. The Buccaneers’ passing attack has been a disaster this year, and it’s hard to figure out why. For the year, they rank: 29th in yards per attempt (5.9) 31st in passer rating (70.2) 30th in dropback EPA (-0.129) 31st in success rate (37.9%) It’s been a disaster year for Baker Mayfield. Beyond just the injuries to his thumb and feet, Mayfield has just not looked the same as the game-changer he had been for the previous few years. Accuracy has been a problem, ranking 27th of 31 in completion percentage over expected (-3.3%). His PFF passing grade of 54.8 is 31st out of 37 qualifying QBs. But his receiving corps hasn’t been much help, either. There just doesn’t seem to be any chemistry between quarterback and receiver. Pass protection, however, has been acceptable. Tampa ranks 16th in pressure rate allowed (36.4%), 11th in pass-block win rate, and sixth in PFF pass-blocking grade (73.7). However, they have the second-highest sack rate (10.1%), suggesting both Mayfield and Daniels have struggled to escape pressure when it arrives. For now, I’m assuming Mayfield plays in this game, but if Daniels has to go, it’s good news for Detroit. The rookie quarterback has an even worse CPOE (-5.7%) and worse passer rating (74.9 vs. 63.4). I want to believe that the Lions’ pass defense is getting better, but it’s really hard to know. They’ve faced some very mediocre quarterbacks all season, and the numbers are certainly improving, but I can’t yet say it’s good. Even the data from the last two weeks comes with significant asterisks because of Malik Willis’ injury and Drake Maye exiting one series into the game. Compiled on top of that are the injuries to Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson, but the returns of Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph are a factor,…

title: Aidan Hutchinson shares thoughts on injury: ‘I always come back stronger’
summary: Detroit Lions All-Pro defensive end Aidan Hutchinson took to social media to deliver a message to fans for the first time since tearing his ACL in Week 10 against the New England Patriots in Germany. Hutchinson’s injury occurred moments after a drive-ending sack of QB Drake Maye, as the star edge rusher leaped in celebration […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 08: Aidan Hutchinson #97 of the Detroit Lions looks on during the second half of an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium on November 8, 2026 in (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images Detroit Lions All-Pro defensive end Aidan Hutchinson took to social media to deliver a message to fans for the first time since tearing his ACL in Week 10 against the New England Patriots in Germany. Hutchinson’s injury occurred moments after a drive-ending sack of QB Drake Maye, as the star edge rusher leaped in celebration and his knee buckled on landing. The perennial Defensive Player of the Year candidate will require surgery, and his 2026 season is unfortunately over . Here’s the message Hutchinson wanted people to see: I honestly can’t believe it. I’ve jumped hundreds of times on a football field and never in a million years did I think this would happen to me. But even something like this won’t hold me back. I can ask why over and over again, but it’ll never make sense. All I can do is surrender to the path. Only God knows why and I trust in Him. Very grateful for all of your prayers and well wishes. Two things I know for sure: 1. I always come back stronger. 2. That’s the last time I go airborne 😁👍 Hold down the fort til I’m back, boys. Hutchinson is no stranger to recovering from season-ending injuries. In 2024, he broke his leg and spent several “miserable” days in a Dallas hospital, and gained a new perspective on life . Early signs for Hutchinson are that he didn’t suffer any other significant knee damage, but they can’t be certain until the surgery takes place. If it goes well, he’s expected to have a chance to recover and return to play sometime in 2027, hopefully “stronger,” as he did after his 2024 injury. View this post on Instagram

title: Lions, Bucs  injury report: QB Baker Mayfield returns to practice, feels ‘ready’ to play
summary: The Detroit Lions (7-2) and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) were back on the practice field Thursday, and with the Lions holding a walkthrough Wednesday, this was our first real look at where Detroit’s players stand with injuries. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded. No practice Earlier in the […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 20: Baker Mayfield #6 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers looks to pass in the third quarter of the game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on October 20, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions (7-2) and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) were back on the practice field Thursday, and with the Lions holding a walkthrough Wednesday, this was our first real look at where Detroit’s players stand with injuries. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded . N o practice C Cade Mays (low ankle sprain) Earlier in the week, coach Dan Campbell said he didn’t think Mays would reach a point where he could play this week. With an estimated “no practice” on Wednesday and an official “no practice” on Thursday, it’s probably too late for a player who’s been injured for multiple weeks to return to practice and play in a game with only a few days remaining. Mays is almost certainly out for this Sunday. Limited practice RB Sione Vaki (ankle) DL Tyler Lacy (shoulder) LB Joe Bachie (knee) CB D.J. Reed (hip) — won’t rush back, unlikely to play vs. Bucs CB Khalil Dorsey (ankle) CB Ennis Rakestraw (shoulder) Vaki has been nursing his ankle injury for nearly two weeks, but he hasn’t missed any game time and practiced this week, suggesting he could play again on Sunday. Lacy’s best asset is his ability to stop the run, and with the Bucs grinding out yards on the ground, he’d give the Lions a big boost if he is available to play on Sunday—which sounds realistic based on how coaches have been discussing him this week. Bachie has been solid special teams depth since being called up to the active roster, but little is known about his injury. If he can’t play, the Lions have five other linebackers on the active roster and Owen Pappoe (elevated for special teams last week) on the practice squad. Reed is getting some work on the practice field this week, but he is taking his recovery process slowly after rushing back too soon last year. It wouldn’t be surprising to see Reed sit out another week and potentially work toward trying to be ready for the Bears on Thanksgiving. “I definitely want to make sure I come back and I feel like myself. I don’t want to rush it, especially because our defense is playing well,” Reed said. “So I don’t want to be a hindrance. So I just gotta be honest with myself, be honest with the trainers and my coaches to see if I’m ready to go, whenever that is.” Dorsey was injured during the Patriots game and needed trainers’ assistance, but he exited the field on his own and is estimated to have practiced on Wednesday, an encouraging sign for his potential availability against the Bucs. Rakestraw did not appear to suffer an injury against the Patriots, but he played only a few snaps, so the injury may have been nagging. Like Dorsey, limited practices are encouraging signs for his potential availability. Full practice S Kerby Joseph (knee) Joseph continues to take the necessary steps to return to game action this Sunday, as Campbell noted earlier in the week. As long as he doesn’t suffer any setbacks between now and Sunday, expect him to play against the Bucs. Bucs’ injury report No practice RB Bucky Irving (rest) WR Chris Godwin (rest) S Antoine Winfield Jr. (ankle) Limited QB Baker Mayfield (foot/right thumb) — UPGRADED from no practice Wednesday DT A’Shawn Robinson (rest) OLB Yaya Diaby (knee) Full CB Josh Hayes (knee) TE Cade Otton (thumb) OT Tristan Wirfs (toe) Bucs QB Baker Mayfield returned to practice on Thursday and has a real chance to play against the Lions on Sunday. Some questioned whether Mayfield would need another week to recover from his foot injury, and after missing Wednesday’s practice, things looked grim. But he returned on Thursday and reportedly looks great and feels “ready” to play on Sunday. “I feel ready,” Baker Mayfield says of Sunday and his recovery from a foot injury. — Greg Auman (@gregauman) November 19, 2026 Video: Bucs QB Baker Mayfield back at practice today and even hopping through ball security drills. Big step toward playing Sunday. Antoine Winfield (ankle) still not practicing. pic.twitter.com/nxXn2Eykrt — Greg Auman (@gregauman) November 19, 2026

title: 6 takeaways from Detroit Lions coordinators prior to Bucs game
summary: Detroit Lions coordinators met with the media on Thursday in preparation for their big game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers this week. Here are six takeaways I had from Drew Petzing, Kelvin Sheppard, and Dave Fipp. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing Kyle Juszczyk inspired how the Lions use Sam LaPorta Recently, the Lions have utilized a […]
full_text: Aug 2, 2026; Allen Park, MI, USA; Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard addressed the media at Meijer Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Paul Barnick-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Detroit Lions coordinators met with the media on Thursday in preparation for their big game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers this week. Here are six takeaways I had from Drew Petzing, Kelvin Sheppard, and Dave Fipp. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing Kyle Juszczyk inspired how the Lions use Sam LaPorta Recently, the Lions have utilized a lot of return motions with Sam LaPorta—where he’ll be in motion in one direction during the snap, and suddenly change directions after the snap. Here’s a good example from last week: The Lions are getting really good at using this "Banana" motion. Fun G/H counter variation with it and it works so well for RB Sione Vaki to follow a lead blocker and get downhill. #OnePride pic.twitter.com/Ho0OGk5En0 — Russell Brown (@RussNFLDraft) November 16, 2026 Petzing revealed that he was inspired by how the 49ers use fullback Kyle Juszczyk—someone Petzing worked with at Harvard—when putting LaPorta in that role. “You have got to have somebody who’s athletic, who can play on the move, who can live in the gray a little bit because it’s not like when he’s going in full motion, he knows exactly what the look is or exactly where everybody’s lined up,” Petzing said. “And I think Sam does such a good job of navigating that. And then there’s pass game stuff that comes off of it, obviously, which Sam is elite at. So, I think that’s kind of where it came from and why we feel like it really fits us and him as a player.” Here’s Juszcyzk doing something similar (albeit with no pre-snap motion)—against the Lions—but building some of the pass game stuff Petzing was referring to. Kyle Juszczyk is so good at this I-Formation Wide Zone Lead, but the Fullback redirects to the Slide Route 😳 pic.twitter.com/9bv8kAgQze — Coach Dan Casey (@CoachDanCasey) December 31, 2024 Pass protection imbalance Our own Al Karsten was one of the first to notice some incredible splits between the first and second half pass protection. In short, the Lions have been one of the worst pass protecting units in the first half and one of the best in the second: Detroit Lions Pass Protection Entering Week 9: 1st Half • Sack Rate: 9.0% (29th) • Pressure Rate: 41.7% (24th) 2nd Half • Sack Rate: 2.5% (3rd) • Pressure Rate: 29.2% (2nd) The Dolphins defense entered Week 9 ranked 28th in sack rate (4.1%) and is somehow making life hell… — Al Karsten (@FootballGuy_Al) November 8, 2026 The Lions have allowed 21 sacks this season, and 18 of them have come in the first half. Petzing had several explanations for the phenomenon. “A lot of it is we’ve really ended the last five or six games running the ball probably 70 to 75 percent of the game, which probably has a little bit of hand in that,” Petzing said. “I think settling in is a part of that. I like to think that we wear on people and bring fatigue in the way that we play and the way that we go through a game. So, some of those things could certainly play into it. And then part of it’s probably just chance, a little bit of both.” Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard Tyleik Williams already one of the best nose tackles in football If you were just box-score scouting, you may overlook the impact of Lions 2025 first-round pick Tyleik Williams. But the defensive tackle has taken his game to the next level, and Sheppard believes he’s already one of the best nose tackles in the league who is still scratching the surface with his pass-rushing abilities. “I’m seeing one of the best nose tackles in the NFL right now. And things may not show up on the stat sheet but just turn on the tape and show me where an offensive lineman blocks him one-on-one and has success. Rarely to never,” Sheppard said. “And credit to him because he does have a lot more in his toolbox, a lot more in his arsenal where he could be saying, ‘Oh, I need more pass rush.’ He’s never done that. He’s taken advantage of his ops. He knows where we need him for us to play collectively at a high level and he’s doing it.” Despite his high level of play, Williams has only played in 301 defensive snaps, just under 50%. For reference, Day 3 rookie defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard is barely behind him at 288 snaps. That likely has to do with game situation, and the Lions facing more passing situations than run on defense. But even so, Sheppard expects Williams to see his playing time rise soon. “Are we going to try to find more plays for him? Absolutely. He’s one of our better players right now.” Roger McCreary has earned his trust While D.J. Reed remains sidelined, the Lions have leaned heavily on Roger McCreary. Sheppard told an interesting story on why he’s drawn to a player like McCreary—who has his share of doubters, as the Lions are now his third team in the last two seasons. McCreary asked Sheppard not to pigeonhole him as an outside cornerback or nickel—just give him an opportunity to win anywhere. Now, after a strong couple of games in Detroit, the roles have reversed. Whereas McCreary was leaning on Sheppard to give him an opportunity, now Sheppard is leaning on McCreary to produce on Sundays. “He’s worked his tail off schematically, physically to do the things that we want done here the way that we do them. And he’s doing it at a high level,” Sheppard said. “This past month, he’s been one of our best secondary players. He’s been one of our best corners, honestly. And I lean on him now. The same way he leaned on me with that trust factor of, ‘Where should I sign?’ I’m leaning on him now, now that things are hitting the road and that’s a player that I count on come Sunday and he’s earned that trust.” Derrick Moore playing faster Early in the year, Lions second-round rookie Derrick Moore was not getting many opportunities. After missing significant time in training camp, Detroit wasn’t prepared to give him more than a situational role. Sheppard noted that Moore never complained, just put his head down and put in the work. His role subsequently increased not too long after. Now, with Aidan Hutchinson out for the rest of the year, Moore will be leaned on more than ever, and Sheppard believes he’s already rising to the occasion—starting with his two-sack performance last week after Hutchinson went down. “When his opportunity comes, when you operate in that way, when you operate like that, you’re never going to squander that opportunity when it comes because this is what he’s been doing all along,” Sheppard said. “It’s just at a bigger sample size now. But I’m seeing a player that’s playing faster and faster each week. And that was the biggest message to him. We know what he’s capable of. It’s just doing it at a high rate over and over at a consistent basis.” Special teams coordinator Dave Fipp No field issues in Munich Given Hutchinson’s injury and some noticeable slipping on the turf in Munich, Germany, some have criticized the groundskeeping at Allianz Arena for the Lions vs. Patriots game last Sunday. Don’t count Dave Fipp among them. He believes the conditions were quite similar to that of Lambeau Field. “I feel like that field reminds me a little bit of Green Bay, like afternoon, evening game when the sun goes down in Green Bay gets a little bit slick, sort of similar,” Fipp said. “If you wear the right footing, I don’t think it’s an issue at all. We had some guys change cleats early in the game because I think they felt like they were slipping around a little bit. You could see it on a takeoff on field block or rush or a takeoff on a punt rush or return. Some of those guys are in three-point stances digging in. But, other than that, yeah, no factor. I mean, both sides are playing on it. I felt like the conditions were great. Yeah, I had no issue.”

(Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions defense is going through some serious changes this week, whether they want to or not. Losing Aidan Hutchinson for the season will create a ripple effect across the team’s defensive roster. Not only will that mean new opportunities for new players— see: Ahmed Hassanein —but Detroit will undoubtedly have to adjust how they approach their entire defensive scheme. Will they lean more on blitzing to make up for losses in the pass rush? Will they devote more resources to coverage, hoping that if receivers are blanketed a little longer, it can help the weakened pass rush get home? Luckily for Detroit, Hutchinson’s exit coincides with the return of a key defensive piece: All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph. The Lions activated Joseph this week, and coach Dan Campbell indicated he’ll have a pretty significant role in his debut against the Buccaneers on Sunday. With Chuck Clark and Brian Branch playing well right now, could some three-safety looks help Detroit mitigate some of the damage left by Hutchinson’s injury? That’s the big topic on this week’s Midweek Mailbag. Note: This week’s episode was filmed before Campbell spilled the beans and told the media that Hassanein would make his debut this week. So some of our thoughts on him are outdated. Other topics of discussion during this week’s show are: How much of the defensive improvement over the last month is sustainable vs. how much was just poor offensive opponents? Has Juice Scruggs officially Wally Pipp’d Cade Mays? And what should the Lions do with Scruggs this offseason? Should there be concern about Sam LaPorta’s lack of production—and will that impact contract discussions? Jahmyr Gibbs and Jaxon Smith-Njigba are trending towards record-breaking years: who will win Offensive Player of the Year if they both tear down the record books? Check out the full podcast below. title: Packers’ upcoming Wednesday game isn’t their only schedule oddity
summary: The Packers are off this Sunday, but they’re spending their bye week getting ready for their first Wednesday football game in almost a century. We’ve already covered their upcoming Wednesday matchup in some detail, but that got me thinking: when’s the last time the Packers played on every day of the week? If you’ve ever […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - OCTOBER 6: Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10) back to pass during the NFL game between the Green Bay Packers and the Los Angeles Rams on October 06, 2024, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA. (Photo by Jevone Moore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Packers are off this Sunday, but they’re spending their bye week getting ready for their first Wednesday football game in almost a century . We’ve already covered their upcoming Wednesday matchup in some detail, but that got me thinking: when’s the last time the Packers played on every day of the week? If you’ve ever wondered the same, wonder no longer. I’ve got you covered. Sunday – Last Sunday This one’s easy! The Packers last played on Sunday less than a week ago. They lost to the Vikings. It wasn’t great. Monday – 2025 vs. Eagles We last saw the Packers on Monday Night Football midway through the 2025 season, and it was one of the uglier games of the year. On a rainy and cold evening at Lambeau Field, the Packers held the Eagles to just 10 points, but managed just seven points of their own in the home loss. The Packers have a Monday night game remaining on their schedule this year. They’re slated to play the Texans on Monday Night Football in Week 17. Tuesday – Never! The Packers have never played a Tuesday football game (but you can bet your Cheesehead the NFL will find a way to make it happen in the near future), although Tuesday games are not exactly rare in NFL history. There have been 26 Tuesday games in NFL history (at least according to what Pro Football Reference has on the books) and they were relatively frequent up until 1948 or so. After that, we only saw the return of Tuesday football during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, during which a few postponements pushed games out of their normal slots. Wednesday – 1938 vs. Cardinals The Packers helped christen the city of Buffalo’s new football stadium by playing one of the first contests in the new facility, taking down the Chicago Cardinals 28-7. Read all about it here ! Thursday – 2026 vs. Panthers The Packers’ last Thursday night game was less than a month ago, so no great history there. But you may be interested to know how old of a phenomenon Thursday games actually are. The Packers started playing regular non-Thanksgiving Thursday games around 2007, but have been playing on Thursdays dating back to the 1920s, usually connected to Thanksgiving. The earliest non-Thanksgiving Thursday game I could find came in 1950 against the now-defunct New York Yanks football team . Friday – 2024 vs. Eagles In addition to playing on Sunday, Monday, Wednesday, and Thursday this year, the Packers also have a Friday game on the schedule. They’ll play the Bears in their Rivalry costumes on Christmas Day, and depending how the game goes, it’ll either be a nice present or a lump of coal. Sportswriters, start crafting those headlines now. The Packers last played on a Friday in 2024, facing the Eagles in their season-opening game in Brazil, and the terrible playing surface ended up affecting the Packers for the rest of the season, as defensive lineman Kenny Clark dealt with a season-long injury. Prior to their loss to the Eagles, the Packers had been on a three-game Friday football winning streak. They beat the Boston Patriots in 1948 , the New York Bulldogs in 1949 , and the Minnesota Vikings on Christmas Even in 2004 . Saturday – 2025 playoffs vs. Bears Finally, I know it’s a game Packers fans would rather forget, but they last played on Saturday last season, capping off their 2025 campaign with a playoff loss to the Chicago Bears. Counting playoffs, the Packers have played exactly fifty games on Saturdays and until recently they’d done pretty well in the non-traditional slot. Unfortunately, they’re in the midst of a five-game losing skid on Saturdays, including two playoff losses to the 49ers. There’s nothing confirmed yet, but the Packers could play on a Saturday this year even if they don’t end up making the playoffs. The date for their Week 18 game against the Lions has yet to be determined, and could ultimately end up being on a Saturday. If you enjoy the Packers playing at unusual times, you should be rooting for that — if the Lions’ game ends up being on a Saturday, the Packers will have played a game on every day but Tuesday in the 2026 regular season.

title: How to secretly spread your loved one’s ashes at Lambeau Field
summary: (Author’s Note: This post is for entertainment purposes only! If you actually do any of this, you will probably still get arrested and fined. Don’t do it. Now, please enjoy.) Shortly after the Packers-Vikings game on Sunday, a local fan was removed for dispersing ashes onto the field, which is against the local law and […]
full_text: Former Green Bay Packers Charles Woodson does a Lambeau Leap with fans after receiving his NFL Hall of Fame ring Sunday, November 28, 2021, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis. Dan Powers/USA TODAY NETWORK-Wisconsin Apc Packvsrams 1128212180djp | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co (Author’s Note: This post is for entertainment purposes only! If you actually do any of this, you will probably still get arrested and fined. Don’t do it. Now, please enjoy.) Shortly after the Packers-Vikings game on Sunday, a local fan was removed for dispersing ashes onto the field, which is against the local law and can be punished with an $890 fine . I do understand why the Packers and the city have this rule, as it’s hard to imagine a more popular potential final resting place for a lot of Wisconsinites. If it were legal and allowed there may very well be a line at the bottom of section 108 after every game, or worse, Matthew Golden would drop even more passes after getting Grandpa Rusty in his eyes just before half time. I highly recommend that you NOT do this, but if you do, there are some steps you can take to not get hit with a $900 fine, and assuming you and your deceased loved ones are true Wisconsinites, you know they would have wanted you to save that money. And honestly, it shouldn’t be that hard! You people are already sneaking full bottles of brandy into games; you should be able to pull this off. You just need to follow a few simple steps. 1. Understand the risks There is a good chance you get through security unscathed provided you avoid metals and liquids (meaning, don’t sneak in Grandpa Rusty AND the brandy! Pick one!). You need to be at peace with the idea that you may have to choose between not going to the game or having someone confiscated. If you haven’t thought about this in advance, you don’t want to be confronted with such a Sophie’s Choice spontaneously in front of thousands of people. 2. Don’t bring the actual urn. This should go without saying but it’s a mistake to make too many assumptions about your audience. Your goal involves the ashes, not the urn, and so you need to keep packaging materials to a minimum. We’re talking Ziploc bags, narrow plastic flasks, Velcro pockets, and the like. Form over function, my friend. 3. Understand how much of Granpa Rusty needs to hit the field for success . This will play a MAJOR part in your plans, because getting him 100% onto the field is MUCH more difficult than say, 40ish percent, or like, “spiritually” getting him onto the field. If you need to get close, or even ON the field, the risk is greatly increased, and you will need to employ much more subterfuge. If you just need to get those ashes up into the air within the bowl, things get a lot easier. The closest you can get without explicitly breaking any rules is the first row of section 132, which is approximately 22 feet from the corner of the field. Whatever method you choose, understand that you will need to either take a risk or decide on a delivery system that covers 22 feet of ground, unless you’re selected for one of those halftime on-field games. 4. Watch Prison Escape Movies . Films like The Great Escape and The Shawshank Redemption deal with surreptitious debris removal in great detail, and there are many lessons to be learned. The “false trouser pocket system” used in both could be useful even you have some sort of special Lambeau access, but you will probably need to be slightly more creative. You should also watch The Big Lebowski, as there is a lot to learn about ash dispersal and wind in said movie. 5. KNOW THE WEATHER! This is probably the most important point here. If it’s rainy or snowy, abort! Even if conditions are good, you will need to understand the prevailing winds so that you don’t experience the dreaded blowback. Ideally, you can select a seat where the wind is your friend, not your enemy, or failing that, temporarily relocate to a more favorable spot to perform the deed. Near and Far Now, down to brass tacks. Let’s say you’re the kind of person who is happy to play the percentages and also doesn’t mind if a few dozen/hundred/thousand people go home with a small piece of Grandpa Rusty. You will want to be in the 700-level of the south end zone with a strong, persistent wind blowing from the south to the north. You want that wind taking those ashes towards the field as much as possible. The front row of section 750 is likely ideal . Here, you just need to get the ashes up into the wind. In any set of cremated human remains there will be a variety of particle sizes, and so not every piece will be light enough to carry as much as needed. If you are a very weird person and want to ensure maximum efficiency you can run Grandpa through a sieve before arriving to concentrate the delivery with just smaller particles. Because of the way Lambeau works, once the ashes descend and reach either the field, or the start of the opposite end of the bowl, the air flow will be interrupted and swirling, which is why kicking field goals is so tough there. This plays in your favor as substantial total of the ashes should reach the field or on an especially windy day, turn back around over the field in the opposite end zone, and honestly, Rusty would be hard pressed to say you didn’t “spread his ashes” you know? Now, if you want to really hit the actual grass of the field, you will still need favorable or neutral wind, so still pay attention to the weather. There are two main options here, and if the wind is south to north, the conditions are ideal for section 132, which is the physically closest section to the field. However, I recommend waiting for a day when the wind is blowing out of the north at which point you should head to section 107. Section 107 is ever so slightly further from the field; however, I can tell you from experience that there are FAR fewer people between section 107 and the field. It’s often just one guard, and there are rarely cameramen or random passersby. For this to work, you will need at least one souvenir cup from inside the stadium, and maybe more. You should finish whatever beverage you get and then clean it and wipe it completely dry with napkins. You don’t want any ash residue when you’re finished. Then, using the skills you have developed sneaking booze into stadia, movie theaters, baptisms, etc., you need to transfer the ashes into the cup. If you are not a sneaky person or are extra worried about getting caught, use a bathroom stall. People have been sneaking things from one container into another in Lambeau bathroom stalls for as long as Lambeau has existed. It’s a fitting tribute. Now it’s just a matter of timing, and maybe the best part of this plan is that you and Rusty are waiting for a big play together, because this is how you won’t get caught. You just need to be patient, keep the lid off, or at least loose, and then during a thrilling touchdown in that end zone (or for better secrecy, the far end zone), you jump up with everyone in celebration, flinging the contents of the cup high and forward into the air. In the confusion it’s possible no one will notice, and/or that they won’t be able to pin it on you. That said, you may want to surreptitiously start to make your escape at this point. And if neither of these is your cup of Rusty, well the next option is my favorite. The Ice Method There is one method that is even better, especially in cold games. It’s absolutely impossible not to draw attention to yourself, at least a little bit, while flinging ashes into the air, but if you can get yourself into a late December or January game well below freezing, this is the way to go. You will probably need a partner in crime because I think you’ll need at least three souvenir cups, and maybe four, but instead of just flinging the ashes, you’re going to want to add tap water and stir, and let it freeze. There are still some problems we have to deal with as you will need to spend some time breaking up the ice as it…

title: Green Bay Packers News: Parsons’ return imminent but doesn’t solve biggest problem
summary: For all of the Green Bay Packers’ issues through ten games of the 2026 season, getting to the quarterback generally hasn’t been one of them. The Packers’ defense ranks fourth in the NFL in sacks this year, with pressure helping the team rank second in interceptions and fifth in overall passer rating against. Now the […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Micah Parsons #1 of the Green Bay Packers looks on prior to the game against the Carolina Panthers of the game at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images For all of the Green Bay Packers’ issues through ten games of the 2026 season, getting to the quarterback generally hasn’t been one of them. The Packers’ defense ranks fourth in the NFL in sacks this year, with pressure helping the team rank second in interceptions and fifth in overall passer rating against. Now the cavalry appears set to arrive. Micah Parsons is on his way back, seemingly with the intent of playing next Wednesday against the Los Angeles Rams, and his presence will only further bolster the team’s ability to get after the quarterback. It remains to be seen how he will be deployed — expect a light workload for the next few games, perhaps with him only playing on passing downs — but his return should provide an emotional lift as well as a physical one for a defense that’s already playing well. As that last phrase suggests, though, the defense isn’t really the Packers’ problem right now. That is of course the offensive line, where some recent front office decisions have helped set the table for a catastrophic season up front. One can’t help wondering if this team would be functioning better had Elgton Jenkins been kept around for one more year; had the team not invested so much money in Aaron Banks; had Anthony Belton — wait, the front office drafted him as a guard and he’s been thrust in at tackle by circumstance and the coaching staff, so that one probably isn’t on the front office. And then there is that coaching staff. From a poor overall offensive game plan last week against Minnesota to players seemingly having no idea what they’re doing on a play-to-play basis, the offensive coaches should have spent their few off days in a shortened bye week doing some serious self-evaluation. So, while Parsons’ return is an exciting storyline for the Packers, it almost feels like we’re adding the whipped cream on top of an excellent pumpkin pie while smoke is billowing out of the oven as the turkey burns. So let’s get that main course under control, yeah? Packers cut Pierre Strong to clear roster spot for Micah Parsons’ imminent return | Packersnews.com ($) Strong’s release is all but assuredly a move to open a roster spot for #1, and we should probably expect Strong to return to the practice squad if he clears waivers. Grand Theft Contract: Six Worst Packers Free-Agent Signings of GTA Era | SI.com I’m amused by the conceit of this article, but it does illustrate just how bad two of the free agent contracts of the 2025 offseason were. When you get basically nothing out of a 4-year, $48 million deal (Nate Hobbs) and a 4-year, $77 million contract (Aaron Banks), it’s going to set you back significantly. Brian Gutekunst vindicated as former Packers struggle in new homes | Packers Wire Still, it’s not all bad for the front office. Using PFF grades (with the usual caveat on that), nearly every player that the Packers let walk this offseason is having a career-worst season. And the one who isn’t, Kingsley Enagbare, is being outplayed by his replacement, Barryn Sorrell. Packers LB Isaiah McDuffie ‘just doesn’t flinch’ | Packers.com The team’s position coaches spoke earlier this week, but the big comments were about Parsons. From Demarcus Covington: “As he’s been getting ready to play, whenever that is, he’s always been in the classroom with us the whole time, and he’s done a really good job with that leadership portion, helping us out throughout the week, film study with the guys and then also just giving his evaluation within the meeting room.” I won’t mince words: suspending a player when he’s already on injured reserve is an embarrassing look for the NFL. Yeah, you’re taking three game checks, but when it comes to sending a message about actions having consequences, this message falls pretty flat. My boss canceled our 1:1 so I could keep playing ‘GTA’ | NBC News It must be nice. It must be niiiice. Go Pack Go—wherever you go! title: Packers Roster: Green Bay’s emergency signing board
summary: Throughout the season, the Green Bay Packers bring in players for tryouts to either push the current practice squad as an immediate signing or to build a board of emergency players if a few injuries start to build up in the future. Since it’s the bye week, I decided to take a fresh look at […]
full_text: (Steve Russell/Toronto Star via Getty Images) | Toronto Star via Getty Images Throughout the season, the Green Bay Packers bring in players for tryouts to either push the current practice squad as an immediate signing or to build a board of emergency players if a few injuries start to build up in the future. Since it’s the bye week, I decided to take a fresh look at all of the players that the Packers have brought in so far in 2026 (56 in total) and paint a picture of who is still available. We’ll break these tryout players down into five groups: Players who are signed with the Packers Players who are signed with other NFL teams Players who are available to sign Players whose rights have been claimed by UFL teams Players who are coming off a CFL season Players who are signed with the Packers QB Cam Miller – PS WR Coleman Owen – PS, previously 53 WR Quincy Skinner Jr., PS TE Kenny Fletcher Jr., PS OL Kevin Zeitler, 53 OL Mekhi Becton, PS to 53 DL Haggai Ndubuisi – international exemption, PS DL Mazi Smith, PS ED D.J. Johnson, PS LB Jack Dingle, PS CB Elijah Culp, PS S John Saunders Jr., PS The Packers have signed two offensive linemen to their 53-man roster after tryouts (Kevin Zeitler and Mekhi Becton), but Becton was initially signed to the practice squad before being promoted up. Currently, 10 of Green Bay’s 17 practice squad spots have been filled by players brought in on tryouts. The only practice squad players who have been with the team since training camp are WR Isaiah Neyor, TE Drake Dabney, OL Dalton Cooper, OL Dillon Wade, ED Arron Mosby, ED Nyjalik Kelly and CB Domani Jackson. Players who are signed with other NFL teams RB Damon Bankston (Vikings PS) – previously on Packers PS RB Phil Mafah (Giants PS) WR Bryce Oliver (Texans PS) WR Dontae Fleming (Giants PS) OL Cordell Volson (Seahawks PS) – previously on Packers PS DL Gabe Hall (Eagles PS) LB Josh Ross (Vikings PS) S Juanyeh Thomas (Cowboys PS) None of these players are available for the Packers to sign to the practice squad, since they are already signed to another team’s practice squad, but Green Bay could sign them to the 53-man roster as a poach. If the Packers sign another team’s practice squad player, they must guarantee that player’s pay and roster spot for three full weeks of the regular season. Players who are available to sign QB Carter Bradley RB Ian Wheeler TE Cody Hardy TE D.J. Rogers TE Zack Kuntz OL Robert Jones DL David Blay Jr. – previously on Packers PS DL Eric Johnson II – previously on Packers PS DL Isaiah Iton DL Jalen Hunt DL Zxavian Harris ED Cruz Smith – international exemption eligible ED Dasan McCullough ED Seth Coleman LB Cam Riley LB Channing Tindall LB Curtis Jacobs LB Deion Jones LB Reid Williford CB Ambry Thomas CB Cobee Bryant S Kahlef Hailassie – previously on Packers PS S Sanoussi Kane S Wande Owens P James Rendell These are players who are completely on the street. If you want to think about the emergency board, these are the bones of that board right now. Players whose rights have been claimed by UFL teams QB Jack Plummer (Storm) – retained QB Jalen Morton (Aviators) – retained WR Nick Nash (Storm) – draft TE Zach Davidson (Kings) – retained ED Vincent Anthony (Aviators) – draft LB Chris Paul (Renegades) – draft CB Dwight McGlothern (Breakers) – draft CB Miles Battle (Defenders) – draft S Chris Edmonds (Battlehawks) – draft P Jack Stonehouse (Renegades) – draft The UFL just had its draft, which included teams selecting multiple Packers visitors to the league. Players with the “retained” label are 2026 UFL players whom Green Bay worked out, while players with the “draft” label are new players to the UFL whom the Packers worked out before they were picked in the recent draft. Players who were picked in the recent draft are not all under contract with the league yet, so there’s no guarantee they even play spring ball. Usually, the UFL allows its players to seek NFL employment up to the week after the Super Bowl. If players sign reserve/futures contracts with NFL teams, though, they become ineligible to play in the upcoming UFL season, as they’re under contract with another league. Players who are coming off a CFL season CB Zy Alexander (Stampeders) This one is a special case. The Packers worked out cornerback Zy Alexander, coming off a season in the CFL, last week. Alexander cannot sign with an NFL team (would likely be a reserve/futures deal) until after the regular season is over, but he also cannot sign with an NFL team after the CFL free agency period starts in early February. So right now, Alexander can’t sign with an NFL club, but he will have a window when he can be added. He can currently work out with teams, though, as long as NFL clubs file a request with the player’s CFL club (which can’t be denied).

title: Packers waive RB Pierre Strong Jr.
summary: The Green Bay Packers have made the decision to waive running back Pierre Strong Jr. on Thursday. While Strong is a vested veteran, a player who is usually not subject to waivers, those rules change post-trade deadline — as all players moving forward are now subject to waivers. Strong is just the second player to […]
full_text: (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have made the decision to waive running back Pierre Strong Jr. on Thursday. While Strong is a vested veteran, a player who is usually not subject to waivers, those rules change post-trade deadline — as all players moving forward are now subject to waivers. Strong is just the second player to be let go from the Packers’ 53-man roster this season, as receiver Coleman Owen (who was brought back to the practice squad after being cut last week) was the first. Why did Green Bay make this move? Well, the Micah Parsons of it all. Parsons opened up a 21-day practice window several weeks ago, meaning that the team will need to activate him from the physically unable to perform list soon. My guess is that the Packers will try to keep Strong on the practice squad, which is currently full, to give the team some depth there. Green Bay has four running backs on the 53-man roster at the moment in Josh Jacobs, Chris Brooks, Kaleb Johnson and MarShawn Lloyd. Jacobs is unable to play right now, as he’s recovering from surgery on a broken finger on his right hand. The team does not have a practice squad running back, which is generally unusual for the team. Strong and Damon Bankston had previously filled that role for Green Bay this year. Bankston, who has been cut from the Packers’ practice squad twice this season, is now on the Minnesota Vikings’ practice squad. If Strong passes through waivers on Friday (expected), look for Green Bay to ditch a practice squad player in order to make room for Strong to return to the team. As a reminder, the Packers’ players will get back to Green Bay on Friday after a three-day break from the facility. They’ll have Saturday, Sunday and Monday practices to prepare for the Los Angeles Rams before traveling on Tuesday for their Thanksgiving Eve (a totally real thing the NFL didn’t create) game. Below is the current layout of the Packers’ practice squad: QB: Cam Miller RB: None WR: Coleman Owen, Isaiah Neyor and Quincy Skinner Jr. TE: Drake Dabney and Kenny Fletcher Jr. OL: Dalton Cooper and Dillon Wade ED: Arron Mosby, Nyjalik Kelly and D.J. Johnson DL: Mazi Smith and Haggai Ndubuisi (international exemption) LB: Jack Dingle CB: Domani Jackson and Elijah Culp S: John Saunders Jr. K: None P: None LS: None

title: Former Packers taken in the UFL’s 2027 draft
summary: The United Football League now has a draft structure that fans of professional football are used to seeing. Previously, the spring league’s drafts were by position (e.g., front seven draft, offensive line draft, etc.), but now the UFL has a full 15-round draft — giving fans a look at when players are taken, something previous […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The United Football League now has a draft structure that fans of professional football are used to seeing. Previously, the spring league’s drafts were by position (e.g., front seven draft, offensive line draft, etc.), but now the UFL has a full 15-round draft — giving fans a look at when players are taken, something previous drafts didn’t disclose. This week, seven former Green Bay Packers were selected by spring league teams, including some names that weren’t listed among the league’s top 120 prospects entering the draft . Here are the former Packers to come off the board: #23: Cornelius Johnson, WR – Rhode Island Breakers #40: McCallan Castles, TE – Louisville Kings #56: Tyron Herring, CB – Louisville Kings #60: Damien Martinez, RB – Colorado Stampede #83: M.J. Devonshire, CB – Dallas Renegades #84: Brenden Rice, WR – Colorado Stampede #100: Kyron Drones, RB – Dallas Renegades Each of these players has been a member of the Packers’ camp or practice squad rosters, but none saw regular-season action with Green Bay. Herring was let go when Packers players reported pre-draft, but five of the other six players were with the Packers for at least part of training camp in the 2026 season. Cornelius Johnson was in Green Bay in 2024. Interestingly, former Packers quarterback Kyron Drones, who was waived by the team after the first preseason game in 2026, when Drones was 0-of-1 passing with three sacks taken, has been listed as a running back for the Dallas Renegades. The Colorado Stampede will now have two former Green Bay running backs on the team, as Damien Martinez will join Eillis Merriweather in Colorado. For what it’s worth, Martinez was just the second running back taken in the UFL draft, only behind Miles Davis, who went 49th. Drones was the only former Packer listed on the UFL’s top 120 prospects who was actually taken in the 15-round draft. The other five to make the list went undrafted. Those players were: WR Kisean Johnson TE Luke Lachey TE R.J. Maryland OL Karsen Barnhart OL Dylan Barrett Luke Lachey was listed as one of the top four tight ends in the class according to the UFL , and Karsen Barnhart was considered to be one of the top five offensive linemen available. Clearly, their league-level scouting department has some different opinions than the clubs themselves. Warner, St. Louis Battlehawks #106: Blake Shapen, Rhode Island Breakers Diego Pavia, the Heisman runner-up from last season, will likely become the face of the league moving forward. title: Packers Bye Weekend Rooting Guide: Who to cheer for in Week 11
summary: The playoff picture around the NFL is starting to take shape, and the Green Bay Packers head into the weekend of Week 11 with a few extra days off due to their bye week. The Packers are 6-4 and still sit in the NFC’s 7th and final playoff spot, but plenty of games that are […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 19: Chris Olave #12 of the New Orleans Saints catches a pass for a touchdown against the Chicago Bears during the third quarter at Soldier Field on October 19, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The playoff picture around the NFL is starting to take shape, and the Green Bay Packers head into the weekend of Week 11 with a few extra days off due to their bye week. The Packers are 6-4 and still sit in the NFC’s 7th and final playoff spot, but plenty of games that are taking place this week will impact the team’s chances of holding on to that postseason slot. Of course, the most impactful games are those that involve the three other teams in the NFC North. The Chicago Bears, Detroit Lions, and Minnesota Vikings are all 7-2 on the season, 1.5 games up on the Packers. Determining which teams Packers fans need to cheer for is easy when those teams are involved, but that’s not quite as obvious for some of the other games around the league this week. As a result, it’s time to resuscitate the Packers Rooting Guide this week, breaking down each game on this week’s schedule and which result will provide the most positive impact on the Green and Gold. Here’s the breakdown for Week 11. Thursday Night Football: Colts vs. Texans The Packers play the Texans later this season. A Houston win helps their record and therefore indirectly improves the Packers’ strength of schedule. It makes very little difference in the long run, but the game isn’t completely irrelevant to the Packers. Verdict: Texans Sunday Early Games Arizona Cardinals @ Kansas City Chiefs In every NFC vs. AFC game, Packers fans should probably cheer for the AFC team. In this case, it would be pretty funny to see the Chiefs lose at home to a 3-7 Cardinals team. But ultimately, it probably doesn’t much matter, unless you’re worried about the younger LaFleur leading his team on a late-season charge to threaten for a Wild Card spot (which I’m not). Verdict: Whatever, but I’m pulling for Arizona for the laughs. Pittsburgh Steelers @ Philadelphia Eagles There are former Packers and Wisconsin connections on both sides of the battle for Pennsylvania, but there really aren’t any impacts on the Packers here since they have neither of these teams on their schedule. Would you like to see Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy win or lose here? That’s basically what should be your deciding factor since the Eagles are in the basement of the NFC at 2-7. Verdict: Your mileage may vary. Miami Dolphins @ Buffalo Bills The Packers will play Buffalo and Miami back-to-back in weeks 14 and 15. They’re both in the AFC East. This really has no bearing on the Packers at all. Verdict: ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ Tennessee Titans @ Dallas Cowboys The Cowboys are two games back of the Packers, who beat Dallas in Week 6. It would probably take some unlikely situations for Dallas to claw back ahead of the Packers for a Wild Card spot, but let’s not take those chances, even if the Titans are significant underdogs this week. Verdict: Pull for the Titans. New Orleans Saints @ Chicago Bears The Packers are 6-4, 1.5 games behind the three other teams in the division who are all tied at 7-2. A Bears loss gets Green Bay back to a single game behind Chicago, a lead that the Packers could erase (and clinch a head-to-head tiebreaker) by beating the Bears on Christmas Day. Every loss by another NFC North team is a good thing for the Packers down the stretch, regardless of who it comes against (with in-division games requiring a bit more thought, of course). Verdict: Geaux Saints. Baltimore Ravens @ Carolina Panthers Carolina currently leads the NFC South at 4-5, and the Packers have a head-to-head win over them already this season. A Panthers win would help Green Bay’s strength of schedule and strength of victory. But there is an unlikely event that multiple NFC South teams go on hot streaks and get into the Wild Card race, so we’re pulling for the Ravens here to knock the NFC team down a bit here. Verdict: Nevermore, Panthers, nevermore. Cheer for the Ravens here. Tampa Bay Buccaneers @ Detroit Lions Obviously, as with the Bears above, the Packers need every other NFC North team to lose every possible game. Like with the Bears, it’s also another in-conference game for Detroit, too, so a loss there would have some potential tiebreaker considerations as well. Verdict: Go Bucs. Sunday Late Games New York Jets @ Los Angeles Chargers Here’s another nearly irrelevant game. The only impact on Green Bay is the fact that they beat the Jets earlier this year, so a win for Gang Green would give a slight SOS and SOV boost to the Packers. Verdict: J-E-T-S. Jacksonville Jaguars @ New York Giants Who’d have thought that this would be a premium game at this point in the year, especially after the Giants have gone through multiple QBs and now are stuck with J.J. McCarthy? Verdict: DUVAAAAAAALLLLL. Las Vegas Raiders @ Denver Broncos Here’s another AFC divisional matchup that has no impact on the Packers. In scenarios where the Broncos are involved and there’s no impact on the Packers, I’ll always root against them. Fernando Mendoza gets his second start in this one too, and I can’t bring myself to dislike the little goofball. Verdict: I’m pulling for the dweeby rookie QB. Sunday Night Football: Minnesota Vikings vs. San Francisco 49ers This one should be obvious. The Packers need the Vikings to lose as many games as possible down the stretch to catch up to them in the NFC North race. San Francisco is all but assured of a playoff spot already, leading the NFC West by 2.5 games. Let them run away with the division and give the Vikings another loss, since they need to lose three games more than the Packers drop over the last 8 weeks of the season. Verdict: Cheer hard for the 49ers here. Monday Night Football: Cincinnati Bengals @ Washington Commanders In yet another AFC vs. NFC game, it’s probably worth cheering against the NFC team. In this one, however, we have an MVP candidate who Jordan Love will probably have to compete with in that narrative. If anything, Burrow looks like a strong leader in that race at this point, as he leads the league in completion percentage, passer rating, and yards per game. Personally, I’d love to see Burrow knocked down a peg, even if that seems unlikely this week, to balance the scales out with Love. Verdict: Hope for a Bengals win, but a low-scoring game with Joe Burrow looking bad .

title: Green Bay Packers news: Should fans hold onto hope for Trey Smack?
summary: The Green Bay Packers have a Smack problem. Er, let me rephrase that. Rookie kicker Trey Smack has fallen far short of expectations in his first 10 games for the Packers. There, that’s better.  Through those 10 games, he’s converted just 71.4% of his field-goal attempts and missed three extra points. Those numbers simply aren’t […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have a Smack problem. Er, let me rephrase that. Rookie kicker Trey Smack has fallen far short of expectations in his first 10 games for the Packers. There, that’s better. Through those 10 games, he’s converted just 71.4% of his field-goal attempts and missed three extra points. Those numbers simply aren’t good enough. Not to win the Super Bowl. Not to win the division. Not to win 10 total games. But should we kick our Smack habit already? Sorry, I couldn’t resist. Anyway, it seems like there’s some decent historical evidence in favor of sticking with him. For now. Younghoe Koo is an interesting comparison. After making just three of six field goal attempts during his brief rookie stint with the Chargers in 2017, Koo was released. He eventually worked his way back into the NFL and became, on balance, a very reliable NFL kicker. His current career field goal percentage sits at 85.3% and he’s made 95.9% of extra point attempts. But you don’t even need to leave Brown County. Mason Crosby hit a bump in the road in 2012, making just 63.6% of his field goal attempts. The team stuck with him. Not apples to apples, because that was his 6th season with the team. Even still, he kicked for eleven more seasons after that, wrapping up his career at an 81.3% make clip. Look. I’m not naive. Neither of these examples guarantees Smack will figure things out. But they demonstrate that periods of struggle don’t necessarily define a kicker’s career. It’s also worth noting that Smack has legitimate credentials. At Florida, he converted 82.8% of his field-goal attempts and made 10 of 13 from beyond 50 yards. There’s something there. Still, there’s a difference between developing a young kicker and repeatedly excusing poor performance. The Packers have already experienced the consequences of getting it wrong with Anders Carlson and Brayden Narveson (fights off flashbacks). Smack deserves an opportunity to respond, but fans deserve an opportunity to comfortably take a bathroom break during an extra point attempt. He shouldn’t be handed the job indefinitely. He needs to gain consistency rather urgently. He doesn’t need to be perfect from here on out, but if he doesn’t improve, that doesn’t bode well for his roster spot. Packers could find surprise Trey Smack answer in former Falcon Younghoe Koo is a free agent. His career average FG% would be a tremendous upgrade for the Green Bay Packers. title: AFC Playoff Picture: Texans’ leap up after win over Colts
summary: The Houston Texans won on Thursday night, leaping three spots in the AFC playoff picture in the process. That can go away in relatively short order, but with the schedule in front of them and the teams ahead of them, I don’t think it’s crazy to think they can go on a run. So let’s […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - NOVEMBER 15: Quarterback Deshaun Watson #4 of the Cleveland Browns passes the ball while under pressure from defensive end Jadeveon Clowney #90 of the Houston Texans during the second quarter at Huntington Bank Field on November 15, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Texans won on Thursday night, leaping three spots in the AFC playoff picture in the process. That can go away in relatively short order, but with the schedule in front of them and the teams ahead of them, I don’t think it’s crazy to think they can go on a run. So let’s break down the current AFC standings and check out some paths to the postseason. AFC playoff standings with Texans win on Thursday Night Football 1. Buffalo Bills (8-1) 2. Kansas City Chiefs (7-2, 3-1 AFCW, 6-1 AFC) 3. Jacksonville Jaguars (7-2, 6-2 AFC, win over CIN) 4. Cincinnati Bengals (7-2, 5-2 AFC, loss to JAX) 5. Denver Broncos (7-2, 2-1 AFCW) 6. Pittsburgh Steelers (6-3) 7. Cleveland Browns (6-4) 8. New England Patriots (5-5) 9. Houston Texans (4-6, 4-4 AFC, SOV tiebreaker over LV) 10. Las Vegas Raiders (4-6, 3-3 AFC) 11. Baltimore Ravens (4-6, 2-5 AFC) 12. Indianapolis Colts (3-7) 13. New York Jets (2-8) 14. Los Angeles Chargers (1-8, 1-5 AFC, .400 SOV) 15. Miami Dolphins (1-8, 1-5 AFC, .200 SOV) 16. Tennessee Titans (1-8, 1-6 AFC) Explaining the 4-6 tiebreaker The Texans, Raiders, and Ravens go into a three-way tiebreaker where the Ravens are eliminated on AFC record. The Texans and Texans are both .500 in that tiebreaker so it goes to Strength of Victory. The Texans’ wins came against teams with a combined 12 wins while the Raiders wins were against teams with a combined 7 wins. The Texans slip in front for now as the 9 seed. The Ravens and Raiders go into another tiebreaker with the Ravens’ 3-3 record in the AFC beating Baltimore’s 2-5 conference record. The Raiders are 10th. Explaining the 7-2 tiebreaker The Chiefs and Broncos first go to a divisional tiebreaker, where Kansas City wins with a 3-1 record in the AFC West over the Broncos at 2-1. Kansas City is the division leader. The Chiefs, Jaguars, and Bengals go into a three-way tiebreaker and one team hasn’t beaten both of the others, so it moves to the AFC record tiebreaker. Kansas City wins with a 6-1 AFC record to secure the two seed for now. Then the Jaguars have a head-to-head win over Cincinnati to nab the three seed. The Broncos slot in as the top Wild Card. The Texans’ path to the postseason Right now, Houston is two games AND a tiebreaker behind the Cleveland Browns in the AFC and 2.5 games behind the Steelers in the six slot. The New England Patriots are in between, but they don’t have Drake Maye for this stretch run. In the event the Steelers, Browns, and Texans are all tied, Pittsburgh and Cleveland would head to their tiebreaker first. Right now that favors Pittsburgh, which is good news for the Texans since Houston can still beat the Steelers but lost to the Browns. If Houston beats the team on their schedule they “should” beat, they can get to 8-6 with games against the Steelers, Jaguars, and Packers determining their fate. A win over the Steelers set their floor at 9 wins and secures that tiebreaker we discussed. Then you need the Browns or Steelers to lose several games. If both the Raiders and Texans run the table, the Raiders would move ahead in the conference record tiebreaker, so I am including them below even though they are behind Houston right now. Steelers (6-3) remaining schedule at Eagles vs Broncos vs Texans at Jaguars vs Ravens vs Panthers at Titans at Ravens Browns (6-4) remaining schedule BYE vs Raiders vs Bengals vs Falcons at Giants at Ravens vs Colts at Bengals Texans (4-6) remaining schedule vs Ravens at Steelers at Commanders vs Jaguars at Eagles at Packers vs Titans Raiders (4-6) remaining schedule at Broncos at Browns BYE vs Chargers vs Broncos vs Titans at Cardinals at Chiefs

title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: We come to a very special Friday edition of Value of Things as the Texans won a boring 26-3 game on Thursday night football. Boring is good in this case. It was boring aesthetically and boring statistically. It was boring in every conceivable way. but it was the kind of boring that DeMeco Ryans imagined […]
full_text: Sep 11, 2022; Houston, Texas, USA; Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr. (11) scores a touchdown against Houston Texans Houston Texans safety Jonathan Owens (36) in the fourth quarter at NRG Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Thomas Shea-USA TODAY Sports We come to a very special Friday edition of Value of Things as the Texans won a boring 26-3 game on Thursday night football. Boring is good in this case. It was boring aesthetically and boring statistically. It was boring in every conceivable way. but it was the kind of boring that DeMeco Ryans imagined them being before the year started. Obviously, people will want to big picture this thing and they will try to read into it what they will. We’ve seen this movie before. They did this to the Titans and Chargers. Those were two crappy teams that have only found one win on the season a piece. A part of you is thankful it wasn’t against you and also thankful that you didn’t allow them to stick around in the end. The other part of you realizes that there is virtually nothing that you can take from those games and transport it to any other game. As we like to do in wins, we will look at the basic numbers from the game to see if we can see any trends building in those numbers. We will also look at the great, good, and bad from the game to see who gets game balls and what we can’t ignore in victory what we would be screaming about in defeat. As per usual, we will also have our own C.J. Stroud section. Key Numbers Total Yards: Texans 65/357, Colts 48/167 Rushing Yards: Texans 37/167. Colts 17/38 Passing Yards: Texans 28/190, Colts 31/129 Third Downs: Texans 8/14, Colts 1/11 Fourth Downs: Texans 0/1, Colts 1/2 Sacks: Texans 2, Colts 1 Turnovers: Texans 1, Colts 1 Penalties: Texans 4/23, Colts 2/15 Time of Possession: Texans 37:46, Colts 22:14 This was a thorough beatdown and I suppose we can take some solace in that. From a statistical standpoint, this is one of those get right games on both sides of the ball. It is one of those games that will getting you looking at the aggregate and saying, “see, it’s not so bad.” The defensive numbers will be elevated to average and the offensive numbers will end up looking better than we think. Sometimes the aggregate can fool you. The Great The Tennessee Titans game will probably go down as the best defensive effort of the season. There are so few shutouts in the NFL, so that one feels special even if the numbers might not be as good as they were here. I’m not sure what to make of Daniel Jones. He has moments where he looks more than competent. He uses his legs and you look up and he has turned in an impressive performance. Most of the time it looks like this. Granted, he doesn’t have any receivers to speak of and if you bottle up Jonathan Taylor he gets really exposed. I suppose when you add it all up, he looks like a backup quarterback. We’ve seen these performances from Davis Mills too. There are days when you think, “if I squint hard enough and let my imagination run wild then Mills looks like a starting quarterback.” Then, something happens and you are reminded why Mills is a backup quarterback. Jones is effectively the same guy, but because of his draft pedigree he has managed to fool a couple of teams into believing he can be the guy. Be that as it may, the Texans did not give Jones or the Colts any hope in this one and that is what should have happened. Sometimes the great is simply doing what is expected. We have reached this portion of the season. The Good Maybe my eyes were playing tricks on me, but I thought I saw a Texans running back gain more than 100 yards in a football game. It was a Thursday night game, so maybe I dozed off and dreamt that. In all seriousness, this is what the Texans envisioned when they traded for David Montgomery. This was the game they had in mind. If you add in a healthy Woody Marks in the next game (hopefully) then you might actually have something. Of course, some of that might be a mirage given your opponent. The Colts did trade away a number of good players and some of them were on the defensive line. The Texans again leave a football game surrendering only one sack. We have to reiterate that there is a difference between pressures and sacks. You can almost imagine Nick Caley as “well…actually” guy bringing up sack and turnover numbers to justify his existence. I said what I said last time and that opinion has not changed. Let’s see what happens when the Texans face a team that is actually trying to win football games. The Bad There was nothing truly ugly in this game because it was 26-3. When you thoroughly beat down an opponent you could argue that there is nothing really that bad. I would agree with that sentiment as well. I suppose this is a catch all for those few plays where the Texans seem to lose focus. We will get to Stroud in a minute, but defensively they are still giving up explosive plays. There is still the occasional blown assignment and you were just lucky to be facing a team that couldn’t exploit those blown assignments. You might say that we are expecting perfection and that would be a fair reply, but when you are a 4-6 football team you put yourself in a position to need perfection. Focus on Stroud This will go down as a statistically brilliant game for Stroud. He went 21 for 27 with 194 yards, three touchdowns, and the one pick. He did throw one other ball that should have been picked and almost was. The one interception he did throw seemed random and could be written off as bad luck, but it was a case of him trying to thread a needle and failing. So, this was not a great effort from Stroud in terms of how everything looked. The official count has him with a 118.2 rating. We will just say that this is one of those games that averages everything out. There are games where his rating is lower than what it probably should be for one reason or another. The next step in the Stroud evolution is having a sixth sense for what the game calls for. There are games that call for him to be a gun slinger because he is all the Texans have. Then there are games where the defense does what it is supposed to do and the running game shows up. He started off taking too many chances, but settled in as the game went on. The sooner that Stroud can recognize the version he is supposed to be the better he is going to be. Granted, we are talking about the difference between being a top ten and top five quarterback. We are fortunate to be at that point in the Stroud experience.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: Texans dominate the Colts
summary: There is a hierarchy in the NFL. There are organizations that are clearly excellent almost every season. There are teams that are sometimes good and sometimes not and then there are teams that just aren’t serious about winning for one reason or another. The once proud franchise in Indianapolis has fallen on hard times because […]
full_text: Sep 11, 2022; Houston, Texas, USA; Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr. (11) scores a touchdown against Houston Texans Houston Texans safety Jonathan Owens (36) in the fourth quarter at NRG Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Thomas Shea-USA TODAY Sports There is a hierarchy in the NFL. There are organizations that are clearly excellent almost every season. There are teams that are sometimes good and sometimes not and then there are teams that just aren’t serious about winning for one reason or another. The once proud franchise in Indianapolis has fallen on hard times because they just can’t seem to figure out the most important position on the football field. The final score will say the Texans won this game 26-3, but it was both impressive and unimpressive at the same time. It was a tale of two football teams in many ways on Thursday night. Obviously, the Texans and Colts were two different teams, but the Texans themselves were two different teams. There was a glimpse of what they could be with a stifling defense and an efficient offense. Yet, there were the same issues that have cropped up throughout the year. In the end, the Texans are a mediocre football team. They look good against bad teams and they look mediocre against everyone else. Naturally, we will get to the specifics later in the week and into next week, but all in all the Texans came in and did what they needed to do. They won an easily winnable game in easy fashion. They covered the spread. They met expectations. They were the best they have been defensively since the Tennessee game. It was one of those game that will help the overall defensive rankings at the end of the season. Game ball just might go to David Montgomery for the type of game that everyone envisioned for him when they traded for him in the offseason. He carried the ball over 25 times and gained over 100 yards on the day. It won’t make anyone forget Arian Foster, but it was enough to keep the Colts honest and keep the offense balanced for maybe the first time all season. Otherwise, it may not have been C.J. Stroud’s best effort, but it was more than good enough to get the job done. The bigger picture shows that the Texans diminishing playoff chances are still alive and kicking for another week. Baltimore will be next on November 29th. With Lamar Jackson likely out that feels like a game the Texans should be favored in. You dig yourself out one game at a time and this was the first of hopefully many. It probably won’t make many big believers yet, but Rome wasn’t built in a day either.
