title: 5 questions with the enemy ahead of Steelers-Eagles
summary: The Steelers are looking to rebound this week as they head on the road to take on the 2-7 Eagles. We talked with Brandon Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation to figure out what’s gone wrong with Philadelphia’s season, and what we can expect for this game. 1. This Eagles roster is hardly recognizable from the […]
full_text: Photo by Todd Olszewski/Getty Images | Getty Images The Steelers are looking to rebound this week as they head on the road to take on the 2-7 Eagles. We talked with Brandon Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation to figure out what’s gone wrong with Philadelphia’s season, and what we can expect for this game. 1. This Eagles roster is hardly recognizable from the squad that won the Super Bowl just two seasons ago. I think most fans are aware of the Jalen Hurts situation. Outside of that, can you summarize for Steelers fans what has gone wrong for the 2-7 Eagles this season? Brandon Gowton : For starters, I’d recommend checking out Jimmy Kempski’s “ Eagles season from hell ” tracker. The TL;DR version is that the Eagles have been really bad and injured. The new-look offense is even worse than it was last year … and it can’t just be blamed on injuries. The Eagles also looked bad on offense when they were healthy (see: the team scoring seven points in a Week 3 loss to the Chicago Bears). The Eagles’ defense was supposed to be the strength of the team, but Vic Fangio’s unit has largely underwhelmed. Howie Roseman didn’t have a great offseason. In the past, the coaching staff really benefited from the Eagles’ general manager doing the heavy lifting. With the coaching staff now being required to do more with less, Nick Sirianni hasn’t been able to answer the bell. 2. It’s only been one game, but what can you tell us about the Joe Milton experience so far? What can we expect from him and from the offense in general this game? BG : It’s probably not going to be pretty for the Eagles. He’s inconsistent. He has the arm talent to make big throws. But his accuracy and touch were lacking in his first Eagles start. It was good to see the offense ran more vertical patterns than ever this season. But he didn’t actually take a lot of deep shots against the New York Giants. That might change this week, especially if DeVonta Smith and/or Dontayvion Wicks are able to return from injury. Milton’s mobility is also a nice element for the Eagles after watching Tanner McKee be a statue in the pocket. Philly leads the NFL in unblocked pressures this season. While it’s not ideal to often ask the QB to bail out the offensive line, it’s the reality the Eagles are currently facing. He might be able to run around a bit on Sunday. And if the Steelers’ defense has to respect that threat, Saquon Barkley could stand to benefit. But he’s probably just not going to play a very clean game. I expect sacks and turnovers. 3. The Eagles’ defense has seemingly slipped some this season, and the team just traded away Jordan Davis. What’s been happening on that side of the ball? How do you think that unit will play the Steelers? BG : The Eagles’ defense falling off is one of the bigger mysteries of this season. There was an expectation that this could be a top-five unit, if not challenge for the title of best defense in the NFL. This group clearly hasn’t come close to that standard. They have had some good stretches in games. But that usually looks like them holding up while the offense goes three-and-out over and over … before the dam ultimately breaks in the fourth quarter. Other times, they’ve just been bullied, especially in the trenches. There are multiple factors why the defense hasn’t lived up to the hype. Jalen Carter has been hampered by injury and isn’t playing up to being paid as the top interior defender in the NFL. Cooper DeJean unexpectedly regressed after being an All-Pro defender last year. The Eagles have struggled to rush the passer. Riq Woolen, a volatile talent, has had more downs than ups as the cornerback across from Quinyon Mitchell. It’s also just difficult for defenses to be dominant year over year … unlike the case with elite offenses. I do expect the defense to put up a respectable effort. Fangio’s group played fairly well against the Giants, allowing just 19 points. And six of those points came on very short field goal drives (23 yards and four yards). The defense also produced six sacks, 14 TFLs, and nine QB hits. Given Aaron Rodgers’ struggles, I think the Eagles could cause some problems for the Steelers … for a time, at least. Pittsburgh will probably do enough to make the game winnable for them. 4. Philadelphia seems poised to completely reset after this season. Be honest, how likely are Nick Sirianni and Jalen Hurts to be back, respectively? BG : If we’re judging Nick Sirianni by Jeffrey Lurie’s historical precedent, he will not be back in 2026. The Eagles’ owner simply does not tolerate offensive failure. And it’s not just one bad season. Philly led the league in three-and-out percentage last year when the team was much healthier than they are in 2026. With a 5-12 record in their last 17 games, things are clearly trending in the wrong direction. It’s hard to argue that Sirianni has answers or that he’s doing his very best with the talent he’s been given. Even if the Eagles rattle off some wins in the second half of this campaign, I can’t see Lurie really buying into those as an indication of positive progress carrying over into 2027. When the Eagles won four games in a row to finish 8-8 after a 4-8 start in 2011, Lurie called that stretch “fool’s gold.” It became clear that he held onto Andy Reid for a season too long as the Eagles went 4-12 in 2012. And if the Eagles continue to lose, well, I just don’t see how Sirianni survives that. The Eagles are four losses away from tying their longest in-season losing streak in franchise history at 11 games. If they lose out, they’ll have 15 straight losses … the longest losing streak in franchise history (accounting for losing across multiple seasons). It’ll be a total embarrassment that not even a Super Bowl-winning head coach can survive. As for Hurts, that’s a much trickier evaluation. We don’t even know with 100% certainty that he’ll ever play football again since he might have to be on blood thinners for the rest of his life. That’s probably an extreme and unlikely scenario … but we have to acknowledge the non-zero possibility there. Assuming Hurts IS healthy enough to play again, there’s still so much to sort through. Does the team want him back? Does he want to be back? How is his contract situation handled? Who does the new head coach (if there is one) desire at quarterback? Where do the Eagles pick in the first round? Do they like any of the college prospects? How many of those QB prospects actually declare for the draft? I just don’t know how to project his future at the moment. I’m guessing he’ll play for the Eagles again, even if the Super Bowl LIX MVP isn’t going to be a long-term fixture here. But I really don’t know how anyone could feel confident about what’s going to happen. 5. What’s your final score prediction for this game? In what scenario do the Steelers win? In what scenario do the Eagles win? BG : For the first time since 1965, the Steelers are going to win in Philadelphia. It won’t be pretty for Pittsburgh. Aaron Rodgers will struggle against an inspired Eagles defensive effort. But T.J. Watt is probably going to destroy Eagles rookie right tackle Markel Bell, causing multiple Milton turnovers. Nick Sirianni will drop to 0-10 as a home underdog as the Eagles lose this game, 19 to 9. The scenario where the Eagles win? Milton hits on some deep shots, and the Eagles’ defense and/or special teams score at least once. Rodgers turns the ball over three times.

title: Could Gennings Dunker’s return revive the Steelers’ jumbo package?
summary: Despite being a third-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, Iowa tackle-turned-guard Gennings Dunker seemed destined for a redshirt rookie season with the Steelers. Dunker was buried on the depth chart over the summer, missing some time with injury and then opening the regular season as a gameday inactive. Then, in late September, he landed […]
full_text: Photo by Bryan Bennett/Getty Images | Getty Images Despite being a third-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, Iowa tackle-turned-guard Gennings Dunker seemed destined for a redshirt rookie season with the Steelers. Dunker was buried on the depth chart over the summer, missing some time with injury and then opening the regular season as a gameday inactive. Then, in late September, he landed on injured reserve with a reported MCL sprain. Pittsburgh opened Dunker’s 21-day return window from IR on Wednesday, the same day the team placed starting left guard Mason McCormick, who is expected to sit out until the playoffs, on the injured list. And although the Steelers’ coaching staff has said the usual platitudes regarding Dunker’s development so far this season, the rookie’s lack of experience thus far makes it clear that backup lineman Spencer Anderson will be the new starting left guard for the immediate future. Of course, there’s a chance Anderson underperforms or Dunker impresses enough over the next few weeks for the rookie to overtake the veteran in the starting lineup. But whether or not that does happen, Dunker could still play a notable role for the Steelers as the sixth lineman in the offense’s jumbo package. The Steelers started using their jumbo package this season in Week 7, a 16-10 win over the Saints where Pittsburgh rushed for 148 yards. It appeared again in Week 8’s victory over the Cleveland Browns, where the Steelers managed 200 yards on the ground. Anderson, of course, has served as that sixth lineman in the jumbo package for the Steelers in recent seasons, with Pittsburgh making the package part of its offensive identity in 2025 under then-coordinator Arthur Smith. New head coach Mike McCarthy made the choice to emphasize it once again midway through 2026, and the results were still overwhelmingly positive. According to Sumer Sports, Pittsburgh averages +0.25 EPA per rush when using its jumbo package in 11 personnel this season, well above the team’s still-good +0.06 EPA per rush across all personnel. Per a detailed breakdown from BTSC’s Ryan Parish following the Browns game, the Steelers earned a first down or touchdown on 37.5% of their runs out of a six-lineman package in Weeks 7-8. Why did McCarthy take so long to come back to the jumbo package? A number of reasons could be in play, including game-by-game matchups and Pittsburgh’s rash of wide receiver injuries in recent weeks. However, McCarthy also hinted after the Saints game that the team didn’t use the package early as Anderson began the season in the starting lineup before suffering a reported bone chip injury in late September. Once Brock Hoffman took over as a starting guard and Anderson was healthy again, the latter was available to play as the sixth lineman and the jumbo package suddenly reappeared. With Anderson about to go back into the starting lineup, it might not be a great sign for the future of the jumbo package. But Dunker might be able to fill that role. The Steelers seem to like Anderson as the sixth lineman because his athleticism (9.35 RAS as a guard) and versatility make him a strong candidate for the almost pseudo-tight end nature position. Dowdle 9 yd TD run McCormick/Fraizer double & climb + Hoffman/Iheanachor double & climb + Fautanu & Washington on islands to set the edges + Anderson in motion to lead block through C gap. Hoffman loses his guy so Rico makes him miss, then takes the knifing in CB for a ride pic.twitter.com/cYmCvI4cHW — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) November 2, 2026 The Steelers didn’t seem to like Hoffman in that role while Anderson was the starter as the former scored just a 4.19 RAS at guard and has largely been an interior player over his career. Those same concerns shouldn’t apply as much to Dunker, who has a 9.61 RAS as a guard after playing tackle during his Iowa days. And while Dunker is still learning as a pass blocker, his road-grading ability in the run game should translate to the pros more immediately. Every Gennings Dunker run block rep vs. the Bills in preseason Week 3: Man, Dunker is an absolute bully. #Steelers pic.twitter.com/869EufoaxQ — Tommy Jaggi (@TommyJaggi) August 28, 2026 Beyond that, Dunker’s mean demeanor in the ground game fits perfectly with the bully-ball identity of the Steelers’ jumbo package. Despite Pittsburgh moving Anderson back into the starting lineup following McCormick’s injury, the pending activation of Dunker might not spell the end to one of the Steelers’ most successful offensive packages this season. And facing a bottom-10 rushing defense in the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 11, Sunday’s game could be a good place to start.

title: Steelers insider believes Drew Allar will be 2027 Week 1 starter
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers selected quarterback Drew Allar out of Penn State 76th overall in the 2026 NFL Draft. The selection surprised some, as it was widely known that Aaron Rodgers would return to the team despite not officially signing by the time the Steelers selected Allar. The Steelers had also brought back longtime backup quarterback […]
full_text: (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers selected quarterback Drew Allar out of Penn State 76th overall in the 2026 NFL Draft. The selection surprised some, as it was widely known that Aaron Rodgers would return to the team despite not officially signing by the time the Steelers selected Allar. The Steelers had also brought back longtime backup quarterback Mason Rudolph and had selected Will Howard in the fifth round just one year prior. Now, it seems like Allar might be in pole position to be the Steelers starter come Week 1 of the 2027 NFL season. Mark Kaboly of The Pat McAfee Show took to his X account to say he believes the chances of Allar being the starter are higher than anyone wants to admit. “At this moment, I would say that Drew Allar has an 87.9% chance of being the Steelers’ starting quarterback in Week 1 of 2027,” Kaboly said on his X account. At this moment, I would say that Drew Allar has an 87.9% chance of being the Steelers' starting quarterback in Week 1 of 2027. — Mark Kaboly (@MarkKaboly) November 13, 2026 Allar went 30/54 passing for 351 yards and two touchdown passes in his three preseason appearances. The biggest takeaway from his preseason performance was how well Allar took care of the ball while also making noticeable strides with his footwork. With Aaron Rodgers retiring after the season, and Mason Rudolph on an expiring contract, it leaves the team with just Allar and Howard under contract for 2027. With the Steelers firmly in playoff position, the likelihood of them selecting a top quarterback in a weird 2027 quarterback draft class is low. Given the fact that Mike McCarthy picked Allar himself, his strong preseason showing, and all of the progress being made behind the scenes, insiders are starting to believe we could very well he headed for number 16 to be under center for the Steelers come Week 1 of the 2027 NFL season. title: Puka Nacua won’t play vs. Seahawks after ‘likely’ season-ending MCL surgery
summary: After Thursday’s news that Los Angeles Rams star receiver Puka Nacua’s league-imposed 3-game suspension would be served while on injured reserve, it turns out Nacua’s next game will probably be in the 2027 season anyway. Rams head coach Sean McVay said on Friday that Nacua, who was placed on IR following MCL and PCL sprains […]
full_text: After Thursday’s news that Los Angeles Rams star receiver Puka Nacua’s league-imposed 3-game suspension would be served while on injured reserve , it turns out Nacua’s next game will probably be in the 2027 season anyway. Rams head coach Sean McVay said on Friday that Nacua, who was placed on IR following MCL and PCL sprains (plus turf toe), will undergo what is likely season-ending knee surgery. Rams star WR Puka Nacua will undergo MCL surgery and is likely going to miss the rest of the season. He'll be out "a couple months," per Sean McVay. — Nate Atkins (@NateAtkins_) November 20, 2026 Nacua sustained the injury on a very needless 3rd and 11 handoff when trying to run the clock out against the Washington Commanders. Keep in mind that Nacua was already targeted 19 times and caught 14 passes in this game, in addition to taking a handoff earlier in the contest. All-Pro WR Puka Nacua suffered a knee injury on the Rams’ final offensive snap today, and will undergo an MRI on Monday to determine the extent of the injury, per @MikeGarafolo and me. The team does not believe he suffered a torn ACL, but the imaging Monday will tell more. pic.twitter.com/S264w2Fe0A — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) November 8, 2026 The surgery news obviously means that, barring one hell of an overestimation of his recovery timeline, Nacua will not play against the Seattle Seahawks in Weeks 16 or 18, which could be critical matchups as far as making the playoffs. Davante Adams should be back within the next few weeks after rupturing his hamstring, but if he’s not back any time soon then the Rams could go into upcoming games against the Green Bay packers, Kansas City Chiefs, and San Francisco 49ers without their top two receivers, not to mention injuries to offensive linemen Steve Avila and Coleman Shelton. LA’s dream superteam is steadily falling apart, and there’s no guarantee at this point that the Christmas Day showdown at Lumen Field will even have playoff implications for the Rams at this stage. Their fate may actually come down to their defense and the Myles Garrett/Aaron Donald combo to step up in the face of a likely passing offense dropoff.

title: 7 former Seahawks chosen in the 2027 UFL Draft
summary: The 2027 UFL Draft wrapped up Thursday, with six players who previously spent time with the Seattle Seahawks selected across the 15-round event. The group includes a former seventh-round NFL draft pick, a former fifth-round Los Angeles Rams selection, several undrafted free agents and players who spent time with Seattle during training camp or on […]
full_text: The 2027 UFL Draft wrapped up Thursday, with six players who previously spent time with the Seattle Seahawks selected across the 15-round event. The group includes a former seventh-round NFL draft pick, a former fifth-round Los Angeles Rams selection, several undrafted free agents and players who spent time with Seattle during training camp or on the practice squad. Not all of them appeared in a regular-season game for the Seahawks, but each had a connection to the organization. Here is a closer look at their time in Seattle and where they are headed next. Marvin Jones Jr. – Dallas Renegades Edge rusher | No. 11 overall | Second round Jones joined Seattle as an undrafted free agent in May 2026 after finishing his college career at Oklahoma. He spent time with the team during the offseason and eventually earned another opportunity on the practice squad in August. His second stint didn’t last long, as Seattle released him on September 5. Dallas made Jones one of its earliest selections, taking him 11th overall in the second round. Derrick Graham – St. Louis Battlehawks Offensive tackle | No. 13 overall | Second round Graham’s time in Seattle was brief. The Tulane offensive tackle originally signed with the Houston Texans as an undrafted free agent in June 2026. After leaving Houston, he received an opportunity with the Seahawks. Seattle signed him on August 25, but released him just four days later. He never made it to a regular-season game with the team. Jalan Gaines – Orlando Storm Edge rusher | No. 14 overall | Second round Gaines joined Seattle as an undrafted free agent in May 2025 after playing at Illinois State. He quickly made an impression during his first preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders. With the game tied 23-23 and time expiring, Gaines blocked Daniel Carlson’s 55-yard field goal attempt , preserving the tie and denying Pete Carroll a victory in his return to Lumen Field. That wasn’t his only encouraging moment. Gaines continued to flash during training camp, showing some pass-rush ability and the kind of athleticism that made him an intriguing developmental prospect. He eventually spent time on the practice squad before signing a future contract with Seattle in February 2026. The Seahawks gave him another opportunity, but he couldn’t secure a permanent roster spot. Chris Paul Jr. – Dallas Renegades Linebacker | No. 18 overall | Third round Paul Jr. arrived in Seattle with an interesting background. The Los Angeles Rams selected him in the fifth round of the 2025 NFL Draft, 172nd overall, before waiving him. The former Ole Miss linebacker had a strong final college season, recording 88 tackles, 11 tackles for loss and 3.5 sacks in 2024. He earned All-American recognition and was a Butkus Award finalist. There was reason to believe Paul could develop into a useful NFL linebacker. He joined Seattle in 2026 and showed some of that potential during the preseason. His best performance came against the Tennessee Titans in Week 2 of this year. Paul recorded eight total tackles, six of them solo, and added a tackle for loss. He was one of Seattle’s more productive defensive players that night. Unfortunately, his opportunity came to an abrupt end. Paul was waived with an injury designation on August 27, following the Titans game. He never got the chance to establish himself in Seattle’s regular-season defense. J.R. Singleton – Orlando Storm Defensive tackle | No. 46 overall | Sixth round Singleton joined Seattle as an undrafted free agent after the 2025 NFL Draft, coming out of Iowa State. He spent time with the Seahawks during training camp and the preseason, showing flashes as an interior defensive lineman. His ability to compete along the defensive front made him an interesting developmental option, even if he wasn’t able to turn those moments into a permanent roster spot. Seattle continued to give him opportunities during its offseason roster-building process, but Singleton ultimately couldn’t establish himself as a long-term option. Damien Martinez – Colorado Stampede Running back | No. 60 overall | Eighth round Martinez is probably the most recognizable name on this list for Seahawks fans. Seattle selected the RB with the 223rd overall pick in the seventh round of the 2025 NFL Draft. Martinez entered the league after a productive college career at Oregon State and Miami, finishing his final season with 1,002 rushing yards and 10 touchdowns. He entered training camp competing for a place in Seattle’s running back room but couldn’t secure a spot on the initial 53-man roster. The Seahawks brought him back on the practice squad after roster cuts. His time in Seattle eventually came to an end, and he was most recently with the Green Bay Packers practice squad. Brenden Rice – Colorado Stampede Wide receiver | 84th overall pick | 11th round Brenden Rice is another notable name on this list. The son of legendary wide receiver Jerry Rice, who also played for Seattle late in his career, Brenden began his professional journey after being selected by the Los Angeles Chargers in the fifth round of the 2024 NFL Draft. He appeared in three games during his rookie season, primarily contributing on special teams, before ending the year on injured reserve. The Chargers released him in August 2025, and he subsequently spent time on the New England Patriots’ practice squad. The Seahawks signed Rice to their practice squad on November 18, 2025. His time in Seattle was short-lived, however, as the team released him on December 2 without appearing in a regular-season game. Rice will now get another opportunity with the Colorado Stampede. Other former Seahawks already in the UFL The seven players selected in the 2027 UFL Draft aren’t the only former Seahawks looking to continue their football careers in spring football. Several other players with Seattle ties are already on UFL rosters for the upcoming season. Here are some additional names worth keeping an eye on. Colorado Stampede (3) Mike Novitsky, C: Novitsky signed with Seattle as an undrafted free agent in 2024 out of Kansas. He spent time on the practice squad and signed a future contract before being released in April 2025. Raiqwon O’Neal, OT: O’Neal had multiple stints with Seattle, including time on the active roster in 2023 and the practice squad in 2024. The Seahawks originally acquired him after he spent time with Tampa Bay. Cam Bright, LB: An undrafted free agent out of Washington in 2023, Bright spent part of the offseason with Seattle before being released. St. Louis Battlehawks (1) Sal Cannella, TE: Cannella signed with Seattle in August 2023 after an impressive season with the XFL’s Arlington Renegades. His stay with the Seahawks lasted just six days, but he went on to establish himself as one of spring football’s more productive tight ends. He has earned All-UFL recognition and is now back with St. Louis. Columbus Aviators (2) Easop Winston Jr., WR: Winston spent time with Seattle in 2023 and was part of the Seahawks’ initial 53-man roster. He also returned to the organization on a future contract and was part of the practice squad. Walter Palmore, DT: Palmore spent time with Seattle during the 2021 offseason after signing in May. He also had opportunities with other NFL teams before building a career in spring football. He’s been in spring football since 2022. Dallas Renegades (2) Jalen McKenzie, OL: McKenzie spent time on Seattle’s practice squad in 2022 and signed a future contract with the Seahawks in January 2023. He later moved on to other NFL organizations before joining the UFL. John Rhys Plumlee, QB: Plumlee joined Seattle’s practice squad late in the 2024 season and was promoted to the active roster in January 2025. The former Ole Miss and UCF quarterback was also an intriguing athlete because of his ability to contribute at quarterback and receiver. title: Puka Nacua’s 3-game suspension won’t impact his availability for Seahawks games
summary: Marred with injuries, it’s been a frustrating season for the Los Angeles Rams’ wide receiver corps thus far and already without its top two pass catchers — their situation nearly just got worse. Puka Nacua has been suspended three games without pay for violating the league’s personal conduct policy, the NFL announced on Thursday. In […]
full_text: Marred with injuries, it’s been a frustrating season for the Los Angeles Rams’ wide receiver corps thus far and already without its top two pass catchers — their situation nearly just got worse. Puka Nacua has been suspended three games without pay for violating the league’s personal conduct policy, the NFL announced on Thursday. In addition, the league reportedly communicated to the superstar wideout that any further violation “will subject him to additional and more substantial discipline, including banishment from the League.” The NFL said it also communicated to Puka Nacua that that “any further violation of the Personal Conduct Policy, including failing to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program, will subject him to additional and more substantial discipline, including banishment from the… — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) November 19, 2026 The move stems from an apparent incident on New Year’s Eve 2025, where a woman alleged he bit her on the shoulder and made an antisemitic remark. Although she filed a civil lawsuit against Nacua on March 25, his attorney denied any remarks were made and classified the alleged assault as “horseplay.” Despite currently being on injured reserve with MCL and PCL sprains as well as turf toe , the suspension will take effect immediately — making Nacua eligible to be reinstated ahead of Los Angeles’ Week 15 game against the Dallas Cowboys — one week before they’re set to visit the Seattle Seahawks. It currently remains unclear if he’ll be cleared to suit up when first eligible to return. However, considering the Rams placed him on injured reserve ahead of Week 10, he was already poised to miss a minimum of four weeks. In essence, Nacua won’t miss any time as a result of the suspension. As for the financial punishment, he was fined $961, 167 — a sixth of his 2026 base salary. There is precedent for players like Nacua getting suspended while on IR, although the other examples are not nearly as prominent in the NFL. Puka Nacua’s suspension was imposed when the process was complete. Discipline is not delayed when a player is on IR. Daniel Ekuale, Sam Williams, Mike Woods and David Parry are among those who served suspensions while on IR. https://t.co/oPSdmhNBUw — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) November 19, 2026 In his continued absence, Los Angles will seemingly continue to lean on a mix of veterans and far less experienced receivers — although WR Davante Adams (ruptured hamstring) could potentially return in the coming weeks and take on the lead role until Nacua is eligible to take the field. title: Seahawks legend Mike Holmgren’s Hall of Fame induction delayed… again
summary: The first head coach to take the Seattle Seahawks franchise to a Super Bowl will not make the cut for the Hall of Fame class of 2027. Mike Holmgren has been waiting for 13 years, since first becoming eligible, and will wait yet again, as he saw a different coach advance in the Hall voting […]
full_text: The first head coach to take the Seattle Seahawks franchise to a Super Bowl will not make the cut for the Hall of Fame class of 2027. Mike Holmgren has been waiting for 13 years, since first becoming eligible, and will wait yet again, as he saw a different coach advance in the Hall voting process. Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft have advanced in the Pro Football Hall of Fame’s Class of 2027 selection process following votes by the Coach and Contributor subcommittees. Their advancement moves each candidate one step closer to potential election as members of the Class of… pic.twitter.com/tMEoCW177W — Pro Football Hall of Fame (@ProFootballHOF) November 19, 2026 New England Patriots dynasty architects, Robert Kraft (owner/contributor) and Bill Belichick (head coach) were the choices by the Contributor and Coach subcommittees this year. These two, along with a pool of 13 possible player candidates will whittle down to a group of somewhere from 3-7 inductees to receive a hallowed bronze bust in Canton, Ohio. The aforementioned subcommittees have been under fire before. It was just last year that they drew the ire of many, because Bill Belichick did not get into the Hall in his first year of eligibility. He has six rings as a head coach, and 2 more as a DC. Belichick’s 333 career wins are second only to Don Shula (347) in NFL history. “If he’s not a first-ballot Hall of Famer, there’s really no coach that should ever be a first-ballot Hall of Famer, which is completely ridiculous because people deserve it. He’s incredible,” Tom Brady said. That mistake figures to be corrected in the upcoming induction process. According the the Pro Football Hall of Fame website, “The four other nominees to reach the final vote in the Coach category this year were Tom Coughlin, Mike Holmgren, Dan Reeves and Mike Shanahan.” Of that group, Coach Holmgren has the highest regular season win percentage (.592), most total playoff wins (13) and highest combined career win percentage (.588) and was the only one to win more than 68 games with two separate franchises (Green Bay Packers and Seattle Seahawks). His former players certainly believed in him: Mike Holmgren deserves to be in the @ProFootballHOF : a thread. 🧵 1️⃣ @Hasselbeck : pic.twitter.com/soKq0C2qx8 — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) February 4, 2025 Holmgren was the QB coach for Joe Montana, under Bill Walsh in San Francisco, winning a Super Bowl, getting promoted to offensive coordinator the following season, helping Montana to his two MVP’s and another Super Bowl victory in the Bay. After Holmgren was hired as the Packers’ HC, he catalyzed Brett Favre to three MVP trophies, two Super Bowl appearances and one Lombardi Trophy. He was one of just seven men in NFL history that racked up at least one playoff win in five consecutive seasons (John Madden, Andy Reid, John Harbaugh, Bill Belichick, Sean McDermott and Pete Carroll). Mike Holmgren’s remarkable coaching consistency carried over to Seattle, where he immediately took the Seahawks to their first postseason in 11 years. He won five divisional titles, the final four of which being consecutive and ushering in the Seahawks’ first ever Super Bowl appearance. Under the coach’s guidance, Matt Hasselbeck became a Pro Bowl QB, and Shaun Alexander won the franchise’s only MVP in team history. Some will complain about Belichick’s personal profile as a steward of fairness in the NFL game, but none can argue that he won a lot. Since the Hall of Fame has modified rules so that only one coach can advance, and must run against the contributors category each year, a bottleneck has started to form, that even stymied who some feel is the greatest coach of all time. Coach Mike Holmgren does deserve to be immortalized in the Hall of Fame. If his stats and accolades from above don’t do enough… consider that he has more career wins than many coaches that are already enshrined in the Hall. The wait continues for a Seattle coaching legend…

title: Why the Seattle Seahawks should start Drew Lock over Sam Darnold
summary: It’s interesting that the Seattle Seahawks first acquired Drew Lock in the Russell Wilson trade on March 8, 2022. That deal sent Wilson from Seattle to the Denver Broncos, along with a 2022 fourth-round draft pick, in exchange for Lock, tight end Noah Fant, defensive lineman Shelby Harris, 2022 and 2023 first-round picks, 2022 and […]
full_text: It’s interesting that the Seattle Seahawks first acquired Drew Lock in the Russell Wilson trade on March 8, 2022. That deal sent Wilson from Seattle to the Denver Broncos, along with a 2022 fourth-round draft pick, in exchange for Lock, tight end Noah Fant, defensive lineman Shelby Harris, 2022 and 2023 first-round picks, 2022 and 2023 second-round picks, and a 2022 fifth-round pick, and it set the Seahawks up for future success in ways few could have predicted at the time. Seattle got Devon Witherspoon, Charles Cross, Boye Mafe, and Derick Hall out of those picks, while Lock didn’t quite make the cut. He was Geno Smith’s backup in 2022 and 2023, signed with the New York Giants for the 2024 season , and signed a two-year, $5 million deal to come back to the Emerald City in 2025 . Not much came of it in 2025, as Sam Darnold had enough on the ball to help the Seahawks to their second Lombardi Trophy, but things have obviously been different in 2026. Darnold was injured early in the season opener against the New England Patriots , and Lock finished that 13-10 win, and a 31-7 Week 2 win over the Arizona Cardinals, looking very much like the NFL’s next reclamation quarterback. He completed 35 of 48 passes (72.9%) for 422 yards (8.8 yards per attempt), four touchdowns, no interceptions, a passer rating of 127.3 (the NFL’s highest among quarterbacks who took at least 20% of their teams’ snaps), and an EPA per pass of +0.43 (the NFL’s fourth-best). Still, it made sense that a (relatively) healthy Darnold returned to the field in Week 3 against the Washington Commanders. Dan Quinn’s defense looked like an easy out, and the Lock story was more about the Seahawks having a top-tier backup than any sort of quarterback controversy. In that 33-31 upset loss, Darnold gave us the full Sam Darnold Experience, completing 31 of 45 passes for 379 yards, four touchdowns, two interceptions, a passer rating of 105.7, and an EPA per pass of +0.05. Sam Darnold has lagged (far) behind. From Week 4 through Week 8 as the starter, Darnold completed 95 of 164 passes (57.9%) for 1,086 yards (6.6 YPA), six touchdowns, seven interceptions, a passer rating of 72.4, and an EPA per pass of -0.18 — down there in the mid-thirties with Deshaun Watson, Cam Ward, Jalen Hurts, and Jacoby Brissett. Darnold’s injuries were clearly affecting him, and this was especially true when he tried to throw outside the pocket, which was a big factor in the Seahawks’ Super Bowl run. This season when throwing outside the pocket, Darnold has completed 13 of 35 passes for 162 yards, two touchdowns, one interception, a passer rating of 59.5, and an overall EPA of -12.14 — ninth-worst in the NFL. Basically, because of his physical limitations, Darnold was put on a quick-game plan by offensive coordinator Brian Fleury — his average time to throw went from 3.14 seconds in Week 3 to 2.32 seconds in Week 7, and 2.67 seconds in Week 8. I asked Darnold about this right after Seattle’s 34-17 Week 8 loss to the Chicago Bears — a game he finished despite a quadriceps injury and a cracked rib. “Yeah, I think for me, it’s all about when I get the ball out quick,” he said . “It’s all about knowing where to go with the football. And I think, again, just being decisive, knowing when I need to move on in the progression and doing that. Talking about this game specifically, you gotta watch the tape, obviously, but I feel like there were opportunities to get the ball out, and I just didn’t.” Fair enough, but when your passing game is that limited, it’s a problem. Especially when your run game has been behind the sticks all season long. sam darnold outside the pocket this season it has not gone well pic.twitter.com/BHjc8rr4gb — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) November 18, 2026 So, Lock was back under center for Seattle’s 17-3 Week 9 win over the Arizona Cardinals, and last Sunday’s 21-13 win over the Las Vegas Raiders, and the work was similarly strong. In those two games, Lock completed 33 of 45 passes (73.3%) for 415 yards (9.2 YPA), three touchdowns, no interceptions, a passer rating of 123.8 (fourth-best in the NFL), and an EPA per pass of +0.22 (fifth-best). Now, we have this to deal with. Player Games Attempts Completions Completion % Passing Yards YPA Pass TD INT Sacks Passer Rating EPA per Dropback Dropbacks (with EPA) Sam Darnold 7 211 127 60.2 1478 7 10 9 17 79.5 -0.097 237 Drew Lock 4 93 68 73.1 837 9 7 0 5 125.6 +0.352 102 Drew Lock gives the Seahawks the best chance to win. By the way, Lock’s EPA per pass of +0.33 is the NFL’s highest among quarterbacks with at least 50 dropbacks. And he’s the quarterback who allows the Seahawks to run their entire offense at this point in time. Whether Darnold’s issues are tied to injuries and/or other things, he’s not able to do that right now. drew lock makes this offense better pic.twitter.com/zs1qmj2w9b — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) November 18, 2026 Others have noticed. “Oh my gosh, yeah,” Mike Macdonald said of Lock’s two touchdown passes out of scrambles against the Raiders. “He’s got that ability to extend plays and not put the ball in danger, which is cool. We turned it over twice, but those were really early in the play. Great plays, man. It was awesome.” “Yeah, we just talked about creating plays,” Jaxon Smith-Njigba said after the Raiders game. “Drew’s a creative player, great player, can move around, great athleticism. So, just sticking with him, knowing that his eyes are downfield trying to make a play. Just being there for him.” What Smith-Njigba said of Lock in the wake of Darnold’s possible return revealed even more. “Man — unbelievable player, great player. Not only how he played incredibly, but just what he does off the field and in the huddle and how he commands his troops. True professional, and [I] love sharing the field with him.” And how about an endorsement from Devon Witherspoon? “Ah man, it’s dope. See Drew come out there and do the things he does. We watch him in practice all the time. I call him the Locksmith, because it seems like he’s just got all the damn coverages. To see Drew play the way he’s played, given the situation he’s in, you can’t ask for anything better than that. He comes out here and he works every day. We see the looks that we give every day in practice, man. “We’ve got all the confidence in the world, because we know he put in the work to do it.” By the way, Lock has done all this with injuries to his throwing elbow and his oblique muscles. Download the app to connect with fellow Seattle diehards and share your take. Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . The best man must prevail. Okay. I also got to see what happened in 2012 after the team signed Matt Flynn to a three-year, $19.5 million contract with $10 million guaranteed, and selected Russell Wilson with the 75th overall pick in the third round of that draft. title: Seahawks All-22 Review: The good and bad (and an unsung hero) from the win over the Raiders
summary: The Seattle Seahawks got the win, but there isn’t much to celebrate when you consider the level of competition against the Las Vegas Raiders. Still, this victory was important. It gives the Seahawks some breathing room heading into the bye week, allowing them to get healthy and prepare for the final stretch of the season. […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks got the win, but there isn’t much to celebrate when you consider the level of competition against the Las Vegas Raiders. Still, this victory was important. It gives the Seahawks some breathing room heading into the bye week, allowing them to get healthy and prepare for the final stretch of the season. There was good, there was bad, and there are still plenty of questions to answer. Let’s get into the film. The Bad A defensive start that should raise concerns The first half against the Raiders exposed some concerning issues with Mike Macdonald’s defense. Even against a rookie quarterback making his first career start, Seattle took far too long to make him uncomfortable. Context matters here: Las Vegas entered the game with the NFL’s 31st-ranked rushing offense, averaging just 71.3 yards per game. The Raiders also lost Brock Bowers, one of their most important offensive weapons, during the first half. Fernando Mendoza completed his first seven passes. His first incompletion didn’t come until the second quarter. Seattle didn’t record its first sack until late in the first half, when Devon Witherspoon brought him down after Mendoza had already attempted 12 passes. At halftime, the rookie was 11-of-13 for 90 passing yards, with 21 rushing yards and a rushing touchdown. He had no interceptions. To make matters worse, the Raiders converted seven of their ten third-down attempts, a 70% conversion rate. One thing that helped Mendoza was Seattle’s tendency to overcommit to the run despite facing an offense with such poor rushing production. That opened the door for Klint Kubiak’s familiar play-action concepts, taking pressure off the quarterback and creating opportunities for the tight ends. On the play above, both tight ends end up wide open. Fernando Mendoza pulled off one of the most memorable plays in College Football Playoff history with a quarterback draw in the national title game. Seattle wasn’t prepared for this look. The Raiders spread the defense out of an empty formation, forcing a man-coverage look. Murphy executes a stunt, but Reed is supposed to be the looper and fails to fulfill his assignment, making life easier for the offense as it attacks Ernest Jones. Okada also takes a poor angle and ends up getting screened by his own teammate. One area I’ve found particularly concerning is Seattle’s intermediate coverage. The defense has repeatedly struggled against dig routes attacking the space behind the linebackers. Here, the Seahawks are bailed out by Derick Hall winning with pure power and getting to the quarterback. The offensive line continues to have execution issues If we assume Bradford has settled into a backup role, Seattle essentially played with three backup offensive linemen after Bobby Hart was forced into action. The offensive line continued to show recurring execution and communication problems. Maxx Crosby adjusts his alignment before the snap, and the communication between Zabel and Jones breaks down. Crosby gets a free path into the backfield and makes the tackle. These issues with identifying pressure, adjusting protection, and coordinating assignments at the second level have become recurring problems. Josh Jones doesn’t seem to recognize the play being called here. He initially blocks alongside Zabel before releasing to the second level as if this were a running play. That mistake wipes out what should have been a big reception for JSN. Bobby Hart was thrown into a difficult situation, but considering his recent level of play, things could have been much worse. Once again, the Raiders use their pre-snap alignment changes to move Crosby around. Hart fails to adjust his angle and allows Crosby to penetrate the backfield. As mentioned earlier, these aren’t just isolated individual mistakes. There are broader execution problems across the unit. Hart fails to create any movement and gets driven backward. Sundell climbs to the second level but gets caught between linebackers No. 7 and No. 17, ultimately blocking neither. Bradford also gets badly beaten, and the play ends in a tackle for loss. On the left side, Zabel and Jones don’t execute their assignments particularly well either. It’s worth mentioning that there were some genuinely good run-blocking reps, even if they came against the Raiders. All three tight ends deliver excellent blocks, particularly Kallerup and Barner. Josh Jones seals the edge and even helps Zabel. Sundell delivers one of his best blocks of the season, climbing to the linebacker and taking him to the ground. The Good Brian Fleury: A mixed bag of results This section is essentially a good-and-bad breakdown, because Fleury could easily appear in either category. The offensive coordinator was extremely conservative and methodical, failing to consistently challenge a bad defense in the first half. Seattle went into halftime with just seven points. Route spacing continues to be a recurring issue. Watch where the receivers are positioned as Lock begins to leave the pocket. Kupp and Shaheed are occupying the middle of the field, while JSN and Barner are near the sideline. They’re effectively crowding the same areas and shrinking the quarterback’s options. Here we get a look at a page from Klint Kubiak’s playbook: the Yankee concept. It’s a deep-shot play-action design featuring two vertical routes while the rest of the offense stays in protection. Kubiak used this concept frequently, but Fleury hasn’t shown the same willingness to call it. JSN’s route is excellent, and the safety gets held in place by the threat of Shaheed. As for the alleged OPI: if this is offensive pass interference, Mike Evans, DeAndre Hopkins, and plenty of other receivers wouldn’t have the production they do. Seattle has also been using JSN out of the backfield. The play design could be better, but aligning him there makes it harder for the defense to double-cover him and complicates the leverage and angles for defenders #3 and #31. The inside-breaking man-coverage routes should create space for JSN. And when he gets his one-on-one matchup, he does what he does best: wins and picks up the crucial first down. This was easily one of the most encouraging plays of the game. Lock manipulates the Raiders’ defense, and Seattle clearly wants to run the ball in this situation. He keeps it, takes advantage of Crosby’s aggressive upfield rush, and finds a clear path to the first down. It’s reminiscent of Peyton Manning’s famous naked bootleg touchdown against the Cowboys. Drew Lock had his own highs and lows Lock may have made his first truly costly mistakes of the season, with two turnovers that had a direct impact on the game. The defense doesn’t respect the play-action fake, and nobody bites. Instead, defenders immediately pursue the quarterback. Abe Lucas is slow to recognize the blitz, allowing a Raiders defender to pressure Lock. Shaheed is open on the dig route, with JSN creating space for his teammate. Lock needs to climb the pocket, but it collapses around him. This is a situation where he simply needs to eat the sack and move on to the next play. It’s the opening drive; there’s no reason to force something. This was the most Sam Darnold-esque play possible. Not long after his first turnover, Lock delivers a huge touchdown. The play design is questionable for a long third down, with the routes initially breaking well short of the sticks. Lock buys time, and this is where you see the importance of Kupp’s mentality. He never gives up on the play, while No. 5 momentarily does. Lock keeps his eyes downfield, resists the temptation to scramble, and eventually delivers the long touchdown. It looks like the same play here. The QB had the option to change the play based on the defensive alignment. Horton had either a fade or a slant route; he runs a good route and it would have been a touchdown here. Charb gets a bit lost in execution and causes the fumble. pic.twitter.com/rlbfYZqSPi — Alexandre Castro (@alexcastrofilho) November…

title: How does Jadarian Price’s 2026 season compare to other rookie running backs?
summary: With the Seahawks in their bye week, this makes for a good benchmark to compare how the team and their players are doing in comparison to the rest of the league. Let’s do that with Seattle’s rookie running back, Jadarian Price, and see how he compares to the rest of the NFL rookie running back […]
full_text: With the Seahawks in their bye week, this makes for a good benchmark to compare how the team and their players are doing in comparison to the rest of the league. Let’s do that with Seattle’s rookie running back, Jadarian Price, and see how he compares to the rest of the NFL rookie running back class. Price, who scored his first NFL touchdown last week against the Las Vegas Raiders , is off to a slower start than most Seahawks fans likely envisioned entering the 2026 season. However, a lot of that can be thanks to a chest injury he suffered earlier in the season, one which put him on injured reserve, causing him to miss four games. When comparing Price to other rookie running backs , he comes in as the sixth most rushing yards among rookie running backs, with 208 yards. Ahead of him are Kaelon Black (San Francisco 49ers) with 356 yards, Mike Washington Jr. (Las Vegas Raiders) with 298 yards, Seth McGowan (Indianapolis Colts) with 285 yards, Jeremiyah Love (Arizona Cardinals) with 268 yards, and Emmett Johnson (Kansas City Chiefs) with 212 yards. For rushing touchdowns, Price only has one touchdown which ties him for fourth most, behind the likes of Jonah Coleman (Denver Broncos) with three touchdowns, and Kaelon Black and Seth McGowan, both with two touchdowns each. For yards per carry (amongst rookie running backs with at least 45 carries) Price also comes in at sixth with an average of 3.7 YPC. Ahead of him are Seth McGowan with 5.2 YPC, Kaelon Black with 4.5 YPC, Emmett Johnson with 4.4 YPC, Jonah Coleman with 4.1 YPC, and Mike Washington Jr. with 3.8 YPC. On the receiving end, Price is tied with Jeremiyah Love for third most receptions by a rookie running back (11), behind Emmett Johnson (20), and Jonah Coleman (13). Price is also third for most receiving yards by a rookie running back (91), behind Emmett Johnson (307) and Jonah Coleman (128). Price has no receiving touchdowns. All of these stats show that Price has not yet hit the expectations many have for the rookie. However, after coming back from injury, Price has shown a lot more explosiveness and vision that the Seahawks saw in him coming out of Notre Dame. Most notably, Price has also not fumbled in his three games back. It will be interesting to keep an eye on these stats as the season goes along to see if Price is able to rise in these statistical rankings. One could argue that Price should shoot up these rankings as he will get more carries than the other running backs listed above. However, with Zach Charbonnet also back from injury and impressing, Price at best will be in a running back committee situation. Price has gotten 28 carries over the last three weeks. That’s far less than Zach Charbonnet’s 42 carries over that same time span. In those three games back from injury, Price has averaged 9.3 carries per game, for an average of 29.7 rushing yards per game. If you were to project the rest of Price’s season based on that 9.3 carries for 29.7 yards/game, that would leave Price with 65 carries for 208 rushing yards for the rest of the season. Add that on top of his current season stats, that projects Price to finish 2026 with 416 rushing yards on 121 carries. These projections of course don’t account for other factors such as injuries, weather, game situations, etc., all of which can seriously alter any of these projections.
author: John Tapia

title: 3 areas where the Vikings can offset the 49ers’ strengths
summary: I mean, Sunday night will be everything football is all about. A primetime fight between two of the best teams in the NFC, one featuring the most high-powered offense while the other features the most-feared defense in the league, as the 8-1 San Francisco 49ers host the 7-2 Minnesota Vikings on Sunday night at the […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images I mean, Sunday night will be everything football is all about. A primetime fight between two of the best teams in the NFC, one featuring the most high-powered offense while the other features the most-feared defense in the league, as the 8-1 San Francisco 49ers host the 7-2 Minnesota Vikings on Sunday night at the 49ers’ second home away from home: Estadio Azteca in Mexico City. It’s been a few years, but the last time the 49ers made the trip down to Mexico City, they destroyed the Arizona Cardinals 31-14 on a Monday night. But the Vikings will be a much tougher test than that Arizona team was, being a team the 49ers haven’t defeated since 2021 (and most notably since Brian Flore became Minnesota’s defensive coordinator). In the two games Kyle Shanahan has taken on a Minnesota defense led by Flores, the 49ers are 0-2 while averaging 17 points per in the pair of games. And while there’s plenty to talk about on the other side of the ball (Kirk Cousins, Justin Jefferson, and Jauan Jennings, just to name a few), this week’s numbers will focus on the marquee matchup of Sunday night: the 49ers offense against the Vikings defense: 14.0 Points per game. The Minnesota defense allows 14.0 points per game, best in the league. Two touchdowns. That’s the average game for the Vikings defense. The 49ers have scored at least 14 points by halftime in seven of their nine games this season. And while the 49ers are among the best-scoring teams in the league, Minnesota has shown it’s more than capable of slowing down some of the better offenses in the league. Of Minnesota’s nine games, seven have come against teams that enter Week 11 in the top half of points per game. Minnesota allowed: 22 points to Green Bay in Week 1 (13 th in points per game) 3 points to Chicago in Week 2 (7 th ) 16 points to Tampa Bay in Week 3 (15 th ) 13 points to New Orleans in Week 5 (16 th ) 19 points to Detroit in Week 8 (6 th ) 23 points to Buffalo in Week 9 (1 st ) 10 points to Green Bay in Week 10 That’s an average of 15.1 points per game against top-half offenses. The game listed above that maybe to pay close attention to is the Week 9 game against Buffalo. The Bills are the only team to average more points per game this season than the 49ers. Entering Week 9, the fewest points Buffalo had scored was the 24 it had scored in Week 3 against the Chargers and next to that the 26 points scored the next week against New England. Other than that, the Bills have scored more than 30 points in the other six games. Minnesota held them to 23 points. The 49ers are similar, as they have scored 30 or more in five of their nine games, while only once were the 49ers held to fewer than 23 points, which also just so happens to be the 49ers’ only loss. But it’s not just the Bills: the Packers, Bears, and Lions can all say they have had their lowest scoring output this season against the Vikings. And only the Packers, in one of their two matchups against Minnesota, can say they were chasing a Kirk Cousins-led offense. San Francisco has been held to less than 14 points just once over its last 26 regular season games, but if anybody can slow down this version of the 49ers’ offense, it would be this version of the Vikings defense. 25.0 Red zone scoring percentage. The Vikings’ defense has allowed a touchdown on 25.0 percent of red zone trips, the best red zone defense in the NFL. Oh look, another thing that San Francisco’s offense is good at doing that could potentially be canceled out by Minnesota’s defense. San Francisco is one of the more prolific red zone offenses in the league, ranking fourth in the league in red zone touchdowns (24) with the highest red zone scoring percentage in the league (82.8 percent), despite ranking 17 th in red zone attempts (29). Minnesota’s defense neither allows opposing offenses into the red zone, or on the rare occasion they do, don’t allow teams to score touchdowns in the final-fifth of the field. While Minnesota is tied at the top with the Giants defense with only 20 red zone entries allowed, the Vikings have allowed by far the fewest red zone touchdowns with five (compared to the Giants’ 16 red zone touchdowns allowed). Three-fourths of the time a team enters the red zone, teams score three points or fewer. Only once this season have the 49ers faced a defense in the same stratosphere as the Vikings in terms of red zone attempts allowed, and that was back in Week 5 against Seattle. Entering Week 11, the Seahawks have allowed the third-fewest red zone entries in the league at 23. That didn’t seem to bother the 49ers, however, as San Francisco scored a touchdown on all three red zone attempts in that game. But that’s the thing: while Seattle is good at not allowing teams into the red zone, once teams enter, Seattle doesn’t stop them from scoring, allowing a touchdown on 16 of 23 red zone drives. San Francisco has already done well against a team that doesn’t allow a lot of red zone entries but does allow plenty of red zone touchdowns. Against Minnesota, it will be just as much of an issue scoring from inside the red zone as it is entering it. 67.3 Blitz percentage. Minnesota blitzes on 67.3 percent of opposing drop backs, the top rate in the league. This has been one of my favorite stats to track throughout the season because of how ridiculous it is. Two-thirds of the time, Minnesota sends an extra rusher, which is a whopping 23 percent higher than how much the Vikings blitzed in 2025. To put it in the context of the 2026 season, the New York Giants currently sit second behind the Vikings in blitz rate, blitzing on 37.5 percent, which means Minnesota is blitzing at a 29.8 percent higher rate than the second-place Giants. That difference is more than the difference between the G-Men and the last-place Cincinnati Bengals, who blitz at a 16.8 percent rate, a difference of 20.7 percent. There really is no way to contextualize just how much the Vikings blitz compared to everybody else. So, it’s tough to think about how the 49ers offensive line will handle the frequency of pressure Flores’ Vikings defense will put on the San Francisco front. Only two of the nine games the 49ers have played so far this season have come against teams entering Week 11 in the top-ten of blitz rate, and that was Week 4 against Denver and Week 6 against Washington. But even then, that comparison isn’t apt, as Denver’s blitz rate of 31.2 combined with Washington’s 35.7 rate falls 0.4 percent short of Minnesota’s blitz percentage. Just to record-keep, the 49ers allowed two sacks combined against Washington and Denver but can’t feel very comfortable heading into Vikings week after allowing five sacks to a Cowboys defense that ranks 29 th in blitz rate and ninth in pressure rate (unsurprisingly, Minnesota ranks first in pressure rate as well). The 49ers offense is as good as anybody’s, but no there’s no defense in the NFL quite like Brian Flores’ Minnesota Vikings’ defense.
author: Andrew Pasquini

title: Out of the Den: Nick Bosa has been here before, and Sunday is Week 3
summary: There’s a stretch every spring when the most dangerous animal in the woods is still half asleep. Scientists have a name for it: walking hibernation. For two to three weeks after it leaves the den, the animal is on its feet, but its body is still on winter time. It moves stiffly and slowly. It […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) There’s a stretch every spring when the most dangerous animal in the woods is still half asleep. Scientists have a name for it: walking hibernation. For two to three weeks after it leaves the den, the animal is on its feet, but its body is still on winter time. It moves stiffly and slowly. It stays close to home. But it hasn’t lost an ounce of what makes it dangerous. The muscle is all still there. It just doesn’t move like it yet. Then, all at once, the woods remember what lives there. Nick Bosa walked back into the light in Week 9. Sunday night in Mexico City is his third game back. He’s been here before This is the third time Bosa has torn an ACL. The first was Oct. 30, 2015, his senior year at St. Thomas Aquinas. Right knee. His season was over before the playoffs. His dad, John, said the family was “sick about it 24 hours a day.” Two months into rehab, Nick said something that sounds a lot like him: “I think I’ll be the same player for sure.” He had five sacks as a freshman at Ohio State. The next year, he was the Big Ten’s Defensive Lineman of the Year. The second was Week 2 of 2020, against the Jets. Left knee. He told Richard Sherman later that during that rehab he “felt like there was no light at the end of the tunnel.” Then he came back in 2021 with 15.5 sacks and a league-high 21 tackles for loss. Even then, he said his knee “kind of improved throughout the entire season.” That’s the pattern. He always comes back. It just takes time. The third winter The third was Week 3 of last season, against Arizona. Right knee again. “These surgeries are big-time traumas, physically and mentally,” he said this summer. Then, two games into his return, a calf injury cost him five more. So for all the noise, Bosa has played four games this season. Read the numbers, and you can tell the ground hasn’t thawed. His pressure rate is 12.5%, the lowest of his career. His get-off, how quickly he’s moving after the snap, is 0.85 seconds. In 2024, it was 0.70. In this building, that number is gospel. Kris Kocurek has coached the 49ers’ defensive line since 2019, and everything in his room starts at the snap. Ever since, the soundtrack of a 49ers practice has been one man and four words: GTFO. And that 0.70 in 2024 was the quickest of Bosa’s career. Fifteen hundredths of a second is about a step, and the first step is always the last thing to wake up. Offenses still plan like the muscle never left, because it didn’t. He’s seeing a chip or a double team on 32.3% of his rushes, the most of his career. And the 49ers get pressure on 35.4% of dropbacks with Bosa on the field and 29.8% without him. “I don’t think I’m playing my best football right now,” he said Wednesday. A plan built for a full appetite Here’s the part that matters for Sunday. While Bosa was out, Raheem Morris got creative. Through Week 8, the 49ers lined up five men on the line on 43.1% of snaps, more than they had in any of Kyle Shanahan’s previous nine seasons. Those five-man looks have produced pressure 38.2% of the time, up from 31.1% last year. Then Bosa came back, DeForest Buckner came home, and the 49ers went back to rushing four. In their first game together, the five-man front fell to 21.3%. Over the first seven games, they sent five or more on 31.5% of dropbacks. In the two games since, it’s 20.9%. The four haven’t gotten there. Over the last four weeks, the 49ers have turned one of 31 pressures into a sack, the lowest rate in the league. The rest of the front has spent the week in Colorado getting loose. On Tuesday, six defensive linemen, Buckner included, went fly fishing on the Arkansas River. Their guide summed it up: “The fish don’t care who you are.” Neither does Kirk Cousins. He gets sacked on just 11.1% of his pressures, the second-lowest rate in football. He gets rid of it before anything with claws can get there. And an animal on tender feet doesn’t take the long way around. Tim Ryan, who rushed the passer in this league, said on KNBR this week that he’d like to see “fewer games and more straight rushes,” fewer stunts and more one-on-ones, and to “let these dogs eat.” Give Bosa the same tackle over and over until he finds the move that wins. John Lynch said he expects Bosa to start “impacting games starting this week in a big way.” Walking hibernation lasts two to three weeks. Sunday is week three. And even a groggy animal can still find full speed when something gets close enough. And November is when bears eat.
author: The Coach

title: Brock Purdy is ticking two historically significant boxes for MVP
summary: Brock Purdy faces arguably the biggest test of his MVP credentials this Sunday in Mexico City when the 49ers face the Minnesota Vikings. The Vikings have been a thorn in Purdy’s side both times he has faced them in his career. Indeed, Brian Flores’ defense has been the puzzle Purdy has yet to figure out, […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 15: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers looks to pass during the second half against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images Brock Purdy faces arguably the biggest test of his MVP credentials this Sunday in Mexico City when the 49ers face the Minnesota Vikings. The Vikings have been a thorn in Purdy’s side both times he has faced them in his career. Indeed, Brian Flores’ defense has been the puzzle Purdy has yet to figure out, with San Francisco’s signal-caller completing over 74 percent of his passes but throwing three interceptions and also losing a fumble across two defeats to Minnesota. And the challenge that lies ahead of Purdy at Estadio Azteca is a formidable one, as the Vikings’ ultra-aggressive defense leads the NFL by EPA per play and success rate, Minnesota allowing a successful offensive play just 37.8 percent of the time. Should he overcome it and record his first win over the Vikings to solidify the 49ers’ stranglehold on the NFC by improving to 9-1, Purdy’s MVP case will be significantly strengthened. However, the numbers suggest he is already ticking two important statistical boxes with his performances through the first nine games of the season, albeit three other quarterbacks are doing the same. Per Sumer Sports, nine of the last 10 players to win MVP had a EPA per play average of 0.159 or more, and a win rate of at least 68.8 percent. With the 49ers at 8-1 and Purdy comfortably leading the NFL with an EPA per play of 0.313, the San Francisco signal-caller is meeting both criteria with little difficulty. The problem is that three AFC quarterbacks operating at the top of their game — Josh Allen, Joe Burrow and Trevor Lawrence — are also checking both boxes through 10 weeks of the season. MVP prediction datapoints, updated to include Wk 10 https://t.co/8GdTBIyo3k pic.twitter.com/yhjqc07fFc — Lindsay Rhodes (@lindsay_rhodes) November 16, 2026 As such, despite his extraordinary level of play so far this campaign, Purdy will need to do plenty more to separate himself from a group of players who might have been viewed as more obvious MVP candidates going into the season. The best way to do that is by delivering more signature performances in high-profile games. Purdy’s standout display to this point is his effort in leading the 49ers on a game-winning drive on the road against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 6, while his superb show of playmaking ability in last week’s shootout win over the Dallas Cowboys will also have helped his cause. But it will be the stretch run that decides whether he becomes the 49ers’ first MVP since Steve Young in 1994. Strong performances will be required against Vikings, in the return meetings with the Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams, and in a mouthwatering road game with the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 16. Deliver in that set of fixtures, and it will be difficult to dispute Purdy’s case, and confidence in him as an MVP candidate and in the 49ers as the class of the league should increase significantly if he can pass the Flores test on Sunday.

summary: Jake Brendel, 49ers offense face extreme test against unique Vikings defense“He went through his pre-snap checklist, which starts with him looking at the personnel that the opposing defense has on the field while listening to Purdy’s play call.  When the 49ers break the huddle, Brendel will anticipate the defensive front. He looks at the safeties […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 15: Jake Brendel #64 of the San Francisco 49ers lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jake Brendel, 49ers offense face extreme test against unique Vikings defense “He went through his pre-snap checklist, which starts with him looking at the personnel that the opposing defense has on the field while listening to Purdy’s play call. When the 49ers break the huddle, Brendel will anticipate the defensive front. He looks at the safeties and linebackers to identify the structure of the defense. “If you’ve ever watched a Prime game, the circle around the guy who’s not in the right spot, it’s kind of the same thing,” Brendel said. “There are little alarms going off if the safety is down or the (weak side linebacker is in a different spot).” Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores is known for deploying a wide variety of pressure packages, so the 49ers will face a mental challenge like nothing they have seen this season. Brendel gave an example of the complexities of facing the Vikings’ run defense — let alone their blitz-happy pass defense, which has piled up 37 sacks from 12 different players. “If you look at all the pictures that we have when we install runs, usually it’s five or six pictures,” Brendel said. “But with them, you could really expect 12 different fronts against this, against this place. So you have to make sure you know how to block 12 different fronts.” Nick Bosa admits his 49ers D-line was ‘weak link’ in Dallas, vows it will improve (paywall) ““I thought I could just coast … and focus on other things,” he said. “But I need to, especially with a newer defense, really hone in on the things that made me the player I am.” Mike Evans returns; Jordan James was added to the injury report “It would be Evans’ first time suited up since Week 6 against the Commanders. Evans was the 49ers’ offense when he was on the field. The Vikings haven’t faced a receiver of Evans’ caliber this year.” 49ers Week 10 Trench Grades: Ups and Downs in Dallas (paywall) “Also, if someone came away from this game frustrated by Williams, they clearly didn’t watch the tape, or ignored the fourth quarter. I’m on record as being a big fan of his game since coming out of college and it will clearly take him time to develop as a pass rusher. It’s unclear what his best long-term fit will be. There are potential concerns and limitations, ironically, because of his size. But if you actually watch the tape, he was objectively, obviously good. He was their most consistent pass rushing presence given how few real opportunities Nick Bosa had.” 49ers fans were expecting to see the same Nick Bosa. So was Nick Bosa: ‘I’m going to get better’ (paywall) “I think in the past, when I was younger, it would eat at me a lot more, just strictly the stat aspects,” Bosa said. “But now I’m really just focused on the people around me. And if I feel like I’m playing good football, then I really don’t care much about the stats. But I don’t think I’m playing my best football right now. So that’s what gets to me more so than the actual stats.”

title: Mike Evans returns; Jordan James was added to the injury report
summary: The San Francisco 49ers injury report is out for Thursday. There were several changes from Wednesday. Christian McCaffrey and Trent Williams practiced in full after a veteran’s day off. Cornerback Renardo Green also practiced in full after being limited with a back injury. That’s a good sign, especially less than a week after Green couldn’t […]

title: 49ers midseason awards: Who is the most improved player on the roster?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers lead the NFC, with a critical Sunday Night Football matchup in Mexico City against the Minnesota Vikings. Through nine games, the 49ers slipped up once in Atlanta, and a win over the Vikings could decide the all-important bye week in the Wild Card round. While it isn’t quite “midseason,” with only […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers lead the NFC, with a critical Sunday Night Football matchup in Mexico City against the Minnesota Vikings. Through nine games, the 49ers slipped up once in Atlanta, and a win over the Vikings could decide the all-important bye week in the Wild Card round. While it isn’t quite “midseason,” with only eight games remaining, this is close enough to hand out midseason awards for the 49ers. MVP: Brock Purdy While I was tempted to hand Purdy the MVP and OPOY award, I figured I’d take a page from the NFL voting process and give the MVP to the quarterback, with OPOY going to a skill position player. Pick a metric, and if Purdy isn’t number one, he’s at the very least top five. As for the actual MVP race, it feels unlikely that voters will place their ballot for Purdy over flashier names like Josh Allen or Joe Burrow. Having said that, the 49ers aren’t 8-1 without Purdy’s improved play in 2026. According to SumerSports, Purdy leads in EPA/play (0.29), success % (56.9%), EPA/pass (0.29), pass success % (54.9%), YPA (8.97), rush success % (70.7%), and is second in total EPA behind Burrow (93.69) at 93.09. OPOY: Christian McCaffrey On 364 snaps, McCaffrey leads all running backs with a total EPA of 40.06. Adding in his ten rushing touchdowns, 40 catches, 431 yards, and three receiving touchdowns, McCaffrey is producing a hugely efficient season. The addition of Kaelon Black has only spared McCaffrey hits and kept him fresh. His long touchdowns on Sunday in Dallas show that McCaffrey still has burst. An incredible season following his high touch count last season has been the driving force for the 49ers offense, with the injuries to other skill position players. Rookie of the year: Kaelon Black Unfortunately, Gracen Halton’s season was cut short, and he would have been a leading candidate for this award, but the uptick in Kaelon Black’s play can’t be ignored. Black has 79 rushes, 356 rushing yards, two rushing touchdowns, averages 4.51 YPC, and 3.38 yards after contact. As the battering ram in the backfield, the 49ers boast one of the best running back duos in the NFL. His running style will translate well in January. DPOY: Fred Warner Warner has returned from his injury and been a forced-fumble machine. Accounting for an 11.3% run-stop percentage, the linebacker has helped anchor the stingiest run defense in the NFL. On 549 snaps, Warner has missed just eight tackles and has 22 impact plays. The best linebacker in the NFL proves it day in and day out. His 2026 season is all the more impressive considering his ankle injury from last season. Truly one of a kind. Most improved: Dominick Puni Last season was a down season for Puni as he dealt with an injury suffered in the preseason. Once he fully recovered, his play improved, but it was a step down from his stellar rookie season. With a 5.4% pressure rate allowed, Puni allowed 34 pressures and two sacks, with a pass-block win rate of 91.2%. Puni has allowed 12 pressures in nine games with a pass-block win rate of 95.3%. Finally healthy, Puni is helping anchor the right side of the offensive line with Colton McKivitz. Overall, the offensive line has been very good in 2026, but Puni looks like he’s taking a third-year leap.
